questions.stem: Why does the sinoatrial (SA) node normally determine the heart rate?
options: It is the only cardiac site that can generate impulses without nerve stimulation.
It reaches the threshold for spontaneous discharge sooner than other pacemakers.
It conducts electrical impulses through ventricular muscle faster than Purkinje fibres.
Its cells have a more negative resting membrane potential than ventricular cells.
questions.explanation: The SA node has the highest normal intrinsic pacemaker rate. Its impulses reach subsidiary pacemakers before those slower sites discharge.
questions.distractor_note: Blood supply, contraction strength and ventricular conduction speed do not set the normal pacemaker hierarchy. Other conducting tissues also show automaticity.
questions.dropped_distractor: It receives stronger sympathetic input than any other pacemaker tissue.

questions.stem: Left ventricular pressure has risen to 45 mmHg. Left atrial pressure is 10 mmHg and aortic pressure is 85 mmHg. Which phase is most likely?
options: Rapid ventricular filling
Reduced ventricular ejection
Isovolumetric relaxation
Isovolumetric contraction
questions.explanation: The mitral valve is closed because ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure. The aortic valve remains closed because ventricular pressure is still below aortic pressure. Rising pressure with both valves closed indicates isovolumetric contraction.
questions.distractor_note: Ejection requires ventricular pressure above aortic pressure, while filling requires ventricular pressure below left atrial pressure.
questions.dropped_distractor: Rapid ventricular ejection

questions.chapter: CVS-02 / Pressure tracing and ejection onset
questions.stem: In the schematic left-ventricular and aortic pressure tracings, which labelled point marks the initial opening of the aortic valve?
options: Point B
Point A
Point C
Point D
questions.explanation: The aortic valve opens as rising left ventricular pressure first exceeds aortic pressure. On the plotted curves this happens at B. Point A precedes the pressure crossover; C and D occur later in ejection, and E follows valve closure.
questions.distractor_note: All other labels are placed before or after the initial ventricular-aortic pressure crossover.
questions.dropped_distractor: Point E

questions.chapter: CVS-02 / Stroke volume and ejection fraction
questions.stem: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 140 mL and an end-systolic volume of 56 mL. What is its ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: Stroke volume = 140 - 56 = 84 mL. Ejection fraction = (84/140) x 100 = 60%.
questions.distractor_note: 84 mL is the stroke volume, not a percentage; 40% is the fraction remaining after systole.

questions.stem: In complete AV dissociation, an atrium sometimes contracts while the tricuspid valve is closed. Which jugular venous finding may appear?
options: A persistently absent a wave
Intermittent giant v waves caused by atrial systole
Loss of the y descent with every normal beat
Intermittent giant a waves
questions.explanation: Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve causes a sudden large rise in right atrial pressure, producing cannon or giant a waves.
questions.distractor_note: The a wave reflects atrial contraction; the v wave mainly reflects atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed.
questions.dropped_distractor: A regular arterial-type pulse in the jugular vein

questions.stem: Why does inspiration normally widen the split between the aortic and pulmonary components of the second heart sound?
options: Increased right ventricular filling delays mitral valve opening.
More right-heart filling delays pulmonary valve closure.
Reduced right ventricular filling delays aortic valve closure.
Increased left ventricular filling delays tricuspid valve closure.
questions.explanation: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, often prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying P2 relative to A2.
questions.distractor_note: S2 reflects semilunar valve closure, not AV valve opening or closure.
questions.dropped_distractor: Reduced left ventricular filling delays the first heart sound.

questions.section: 5. How does cardiac muscle relax?
questions.stem: A drug markedly inhibits SERCA in cardiac muscle. What change in relaxation is expected?
options: Faster removal of calcium from cytosol.
Complete elimination of L-type calcium channels.
Shorter calcium transient and stronger relaxation.
Slower calcium removal impairs relaxation.
questions.explanation: SERCA normally resequesters calcium into the SR; inhibiting it prolongs the cytosolic calcium transient and slows relaxation.
distractors: Calcium removal becomes slower, not faster.
SERCA inhibition does not directly abolish membrane L-type channels.
Less reuptake prolongs rather than shortens the cytosolic transient.

questions.stem: Venous return rises while heart rate, afterload and contractility remain unchanged. What immediate change is expected in a normal ventricle?
options: A rise in end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
A fall in end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
A rise in stroke volume with a fall in end-diastolic volume
A fall in stroke volume despite a rise in end-diastolic volume
questions.explanation: More venous return increases ventricular filling and stretches cardiac fibres. On the ascending Frank-Starling relationship this raises force and stroke volume.
questions.distractor_note: The Frank-Starling response links greater preload to greater output within physiological limits.
questions.dropped_distractor: No change in stroke volume despite greater ventricular filling

questions.stem: Aortic pressure suddenly rises. For the first affected beat, ventricular filling and contractility are unchanged. What is the likely effect on stroke volume?
options: Stroke volume increases because aortic recoil becomes stronger.
Stroke volume increases because ventricular filling has increased.
Stroke volume stays constant because heart rate has not changed.
Stroke volume falls as the ventricle ejects against higher pressure.
questions.explanation: Greater afterload makes ventricular ejection more difficult. Before compensatory adjustments, end-systolic volume tends to increase and stroke volume decreases.
questions.distractor_note: Aortic recoil, filling and AV conduction are not the mechanisms determining the first-beat afterload response.
questions.dropped_distractor: Stroke volume increases because the AV node conducts more quickly.

questions.chapter: CVS-05 / Contractility and ventricular function curve
questions.stem: Two ventricular function curves are shown. At the same end-diastolic volume, curve X produces a larger stroke volume than curve Y. What best explains the difference?
options: Ventricular preload must be greater on curve X.
The heart rate must be lower on curve X.
The ventricular muscle must be less responsive to calcium on curve X.
Ventricular contractility is greater on curve X.
questions.explanation: An upward shift of the Frank-Starling curve indicates greater stroke volume at the same preload, consistent with increased contractility.
questions.distractor_note: The comparison holds end-diastolic volume constant, so increased preload is not the explanation; reduced calcium response would tend to reduce contractility.
questions.dropped_distractor: The aortic valve must be closed throughout ejection on curve X.

questions.stem: Oxygen consumption is 280 mL/min. Arterial oxygen content is 200 mL/L and mixed venous oxygen content is 130 mL/L. What is cardiac output?
options: 4 L/min
2 L/min
3 L/min
5 L/min
questions.explanation: Arterial-mixed venous oxygen content difference = 200 - 130 = 70 mL/L. Cardiac output = 280 mL/min divided by 70 mL/L = 4 L/min.
questions.distractor_note: The Fick method divides oxygen consumption by the oxygen content difference, not by either concentration alone.
questions.dropped_distractor: 7 L/min

questions.chapter: CVS-06 / Pressure work and oxygen demand
questions.stem: At the same stroke volume and heart rate, which change generally increases myocardial oxygen demand more?
options: Pumping against a lower arterial pressure
Reducing the pressure needed to open the aortic valve
Pumping against a much higher arterial pressure
Lowering wall tension during ventricular ejection
questions.explanation: Pressure work, which increases with afterload and myocardial wall tension, carries a high oxygen cost. Pumping the same volume against greater arterial pressure is more demanding.
questions.distractor_note: The alternative changes reduce pressure load rather than increase it.
questions.dropped_distractor: Reducing the pressure difference across the aortic valve

questions.stem: According to Poiseuille's law, if a vessel radius is reduced to half while other factors remain constant, how does resistance change?
options: It becomes roughly two times greater.
It becomes 4 times greater.
It becomes 16 times greater.
It becomes 8 times greater.
questions.explanation: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius. Halving radius therefore increases resistance by 2^4 = 16 times.
questions.distractor_note: The fourth-power dependence is stronger than a linear, square or cubic change.
questions.dropped_distractor: It becomes 16 times smaller.

questions.chapter: CVS-07 / Flow velocity and cross-sectional area
questions.stem: Why is average blood-flow velocity normally much lower in capillaries than in the aorta?
options: The total capillary cross-sectional area is smaller than that of the aorta.
Capillaries receive a smaller total blood flow than the aorta in steady state.
Capillary pressure is lower, so red cells are stationary between heartbeats.
The combined cross-sectional area of all capillaries is much larger.
questions.explanation: For a given volume flow rate, average velocity equals flow divided by cross-sectional area. The enormous total capillary area produces low average velocity.
questions.distractor_note: Flow continues in capillaries; the key comparison is total cross-sectional area, not the diameter of one capillary.
questions.dropped_distractor: Blood viscosity is so much higher in capillaries that flow velocity must be zero.

questions.stem: Which isolated change increases the tendency for turbulent flow in a blood vessel?
options: A substantial rise in whole-blood viscosity
A decrease in blood density
An increase in blood-flow velocity
A decrease in vessel diameter
questions.explanation: Reynolds number increases with velocity, density and diameter, and decreases with viscosity. Increased velocity therefore makes turbulence more likely.
questions.distractor_note: Higher viscosity and smaller diameter generally lower Reynolds number when other variables are held constant.
questions.dropped_distractor: A decrease in the Reynolds number

questions.stem: A resting adult has a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg. Using the usual resting approximation, what is mean arterial pressure?
options: 75 mmHg
90 mmHg
85 mmHg
95 mmHg
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure = 120 - 75 = 45 mmHg. MAP is approximately diastolic pressure + one-third of pulse pressure = 75 + 15 = 90 mmHg.
questions.distractor_note: MAP is not the simple arithmetic midpoint; diastole usually occupies more time at rest.
questions.dropped_distractor: 105 mmHg

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, cuff pressure is slowly released during blood-pressure measurement. Disappearance of Korotkoff sounds usually marks which pressure?
options: Systolic pressure in the brachial artery
Mean arterial pressure
Diastolic arterial pressure
Pulse pressure
questions.explanation: As cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure, the brachial artery is open throughout the cardiac cycle and the characteristic Korotkoff sounds generally disappear.
questions.distractor_note: The first appearance of sound usually marks systolic rather than diastolic pressure.
questions.dropped_distractor: Central venous pressure

questions.stem: A deep vein in one leg becomes obstructed, increasing pressure in vessels upstream. What local change most directly favours swelling?
options: An increase in plasma albumin concentration
A decrease in capillary hydrostatic pressure
An increase in lymphatic drainage capacity
Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure
questions.explanation: Impaired venous drainage raises capillary pressure and promotes movement of fluid from capillaries into interstitial tissue.
questions.distractor_note: Higher plasma oncotic pressure or stronger lymphatic removal would oppose fluid accumulation.
questions.dropped_distractor: A decrease in capillary wall permeability

questions.stem: A patient develops chronic swelling of an arm after axillary lymph nodes are removed. What is the main reason?
options: Arterial blood supply to the arm has completely stopped.
Red blood cells begin moving freely out of intact capillaries.
Protein-rich tissue fluid cannot drain through the lymphatics.
Plasma albumin production increases sharply in the affected tissue.
questions.explanation: Damage to lymphatic pathways reduces the return of interstitial fluid and proteins to the blood, producing lymphoedema.
questions.distractor_note: Lymphoedema is caused by impaired lymph removal, not complete loss of arterial flow.
questions.dropped_distractor: The heart pumps excess blood only into the affected arm.

questions.section: 6. Why can't cardiac muscle undergo normal tetanus?
questions.stem: What prevents ventricular myocytes from sustaining a normal tetanus?
options: Refractoriness lasts through most of contraction.
It contains no contractile actin or myosin filaments.
It lacks voltage-gated calcium channels.
Its action potentials can occur only once in a lifetime.
questions.explanation: The long action potential and absolute refractory period prevent rapid re-excitation and mechanical summation into tetanus.
distractors: Cardiac muscle contains actin and myosin.
Calcium channels are essential for the cardiac plateau.
Cardiac cells repeatedly generate action potentials.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.section: 3. Two mechanisms: myogenic and metabolic
questions.stem: Which observation most strongly points to a myogenic rather than metabolic adjustment?
options: Constriction follows a rise in vessel-wall stretch.
Dilation follows accumulation of local lactate.
Dilation follows reduced tissue oxygen supply.
Constriction follows removal of excess local metabolites.
questions.explanation: The myogenic response is the smooth muscle reacting to stretch itself: more stretch → more contraction. Responses driven by O₂, CO₂, H⁺, lactate or other chemicals are metabolic.
distractors: Lactate accumulation is a metabolic signal for dilation.
Low oxygen is a metabolic signal for dilation.
Metabolite washout belongs to metabolic autoregulation.

questions.stem: Blood flow through a forearm artery is briefly blocked and then restored. Why may flow temporarily rise above its resting level?
options: Accumulated metabolites continue to dilate local vessels.
The heart has permanently increased the forearm's blood supply.
The arterial pulse wave has stopped travelling through the arm.
The blockage permanently removed vascular resistance.
questions.explanation: During the occlusion, tissue oxygen delivery falls and local vasodilatory signals build up. When flow resumes, dilated resistance vessels produce transient reactive hyperaemia.
questions.distractor_note: Reactive hyperaemia is a temporary local response to preceding flow interruption.
questions.dropped_distractor: Venous valves now actively force arterial blood toward the hand.

questions.stem: An organ's flow remains nearly constant as its perfusion pressure rises across the autoregulatory range. Which vascular adjustment produces this plateau?
options: Arteriolar resistance falls as perfusion pressure rises.
Cardiac output stops changing throughout the entire body.
Arteriolar resistance rises as perfusion pressure rises.
Venous blood begins flowing backward into the artery.
questions.explanation: For approximately constant flow Q, a higher perfusion pressure requires a higher local resistance (Q = pressure difference / resistance). The plateau reflects autoregulatory adjustment.
questions.distractor_note: Falling resistance alongside increasing pressure would increase, rather than stabilize, flow.
questions.dropped_distractor: The tissue stops consuming oxygen over this pressure range.

questions.chapter: CVS-11 / Baroreceptor reflex fall in BP
questions.stem: Immediately after arterial pressure falls during haemorrhage, which autonomic response follows reduced arterial baroreceptor firing?
options: Reduced sympathetic activity and increased vagal activity
Reduced sympathetic and reduced vagal activity together
Increased sympathetic activity and reduced vagal activity
Increased vagal activity with arteriolar dilation
questions.explanation: Less stretch of carotid and aortic baroreceptors reduces afferent firing. The medulla responds with increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic outflow.
questions.distractor_note: Increased vagal activity would tend to slow the heart rather than compensate for falling pressure.
questions.dropped_distractor: No change in autonomic outflow until blood volume recovers

questions.stem: A patient develops rapidly rising intracranial pressure with impaired brainstem perfusion. Which combination is typical of the Cushing response?
options: Increased arterial pressure with reflex slowing of the heart
Decreased arterial pressure with reflex slowing of the heart
Increased arterial pressure with sustained reflex tachycardia
Decreased arterial pressure with complete loss of sympathetic tone
questions.explanation: Reduced medullary perfusion causes a powerful sympathetic rise in systemic pressure. The resulting arterial hypertension stimulates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia.
questions.distractor_note: The raised pressure is a compensatory response to brainstem ischemia; bradycardia is secondary to the baroreflex.
questions.dropped_distractor: Unchanged arterial pressure with marked peripheral vasodilation

questions.stem: Rapid infusion of fluid increases venous return and stretches the right atrium. Which reflex response may help accommodate the larger venous return?
options: Heart rate may decrease because atrial stretch directly increases vagal outflow.
Heart rate may increase as atrial stretch activates a reflex.
Heart rate may remain unchanged because atrial stretch has no reflex effects.
Heart rate may increase only if the arterial baroreceptors first detect hypotension.
questions.explanation: The atrial stretch (Bainbridge) reflex can increase heart rate when venous return and atrial filling rise. It is distinct from the arterial baroreceptor response to elevated blood pressure.
questions.distractor_note: Atrial distension can elicit reflex tachycardia without requiring arterial hypotension. The infusion increases rather than reduces venous return.
questions.dropped_distractor: Heart rate may decrease because venous return is reduced by the fluid infusion.

questions.stem: Immediately after a person stands up quickly, before reflex compensation has fully developed, what tends to happen?
options: Venous pooling decreases and ventricular filling rises.
Venous pooling increases and venous return to the heart falls.
Venous pressure in the feet falls below pressure at heart level.
Cardiac output rises because gravity pushes blood toward the chest.
questions.explanation: Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure and pooling in dependent veins. This reduces central venous return, initially lowering stroke volume and potentially cerebral perfusion.
questions.distractor_note: Without compensation, standing does not drive leg blood centrally or raise head-level perfusion.
questions.dropped_distractor: Cerebral blood flow increases because the head is now above the heart.

questions.stem: A person loses a substantial amount of blood. What sequence most directly explains the initial fall in cardiac output?
options: Lower blood volume directly raises ventricular end-diastolic volume.
Lower blood volume immediately increases plasma oncotic pressure enough to raise output.
Lower blood volume leads to lower venous return and ventricular filling.
Lower blood volume raises pulmonary venous return above systemic venous return.
questions.explanation: Blood loss reduces circulating volume and venous return, which reduces preload and stroke volume. Reflex vasoconstriction may defend pressure but cannot automatically restore lost flow.
questions.distractor_note: Loss of circulating volume does not directly raise preload or stroke volume.
questions.dropped_distractor: Lower blood volume causes the aortic valve to open earlier at a higher stroke volume.

questions.stem: A patient with severe infection has widespread arteriolar dilation and low arterial pressure. Which shock mechanism is most likely?
options: Hypovolaemic shock caused mainly by external blood loss
Cardiogenic shock caused mainly by poor ventricular pumping
Obstructive shock caused mainly by mechanical blockage of blood flow
Distributive shock from widespread loss of vascular tone
questions.explanation: Sepsis can produce profound vasodilation and loss of vascular tone, lowering total peripheral resistance and effective perfusion pressure. This is distributive shock.
questions.distractor_note: The defining event in this stem is widespread low resistance rather than haemorrhage, pump failure or obstruction.
questions.dropped_distractor: A normal circulation with a temporary rise in vascular resistance

questions.stem: A patient with left ventricular failure develops breathlessness and pulmonary oedema. What pressure change most directly promotes fluid movement into the lungs?
options: Increased pulmonary venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure
Increased plasma oncotic pressure in pulmonary capillaries
Decreased hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries
Increased lymphatic drainage with unchanged capillary pressure
questions.explanation: Poor left ventricular output raises pressure upstream in the left atrium and pulmonary veins. Higher pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes filtration and pulmonary oedema.
questions.distractor_note: Fluid filtration increases with raised hydrostatic pressure; higher oncotic pressure would tend to oppose it.
questions.dropped_distractor: Decreased pulmonary venous pressure

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 2. Where does the blood come from?
questions.stem: Why can a cerebral arterial branch occlusion cause a local infarct despite the Circle of Willis?
options: Small distal territories may have limited effective collateral flow.
Every cerebral artery has a complete set of parallel branches.
Cerebral veins normally replace arterial inflow after blockage.
The basilar artery can supply every distal cortical branch directly.
questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis provides proximal connections, but distal cerebral arterial territories have limited functional anastomoses.
distractors: Distal vessels are not completely interconnected.
Veins drain blood and cannot substitute for oxygenated arterial supply.
Basilar inflow does not directly replace all distal arterial territories.

questions.stem: The cerebral aqueduct becomes blocked while CSF production continues. Which ventricles are expected to enlarge first?
options: The fourth ventricle alone
The third and fourth ventricles only
The lateral and third ventricles
The fourth ventricle and central canal only
questions.explanation: The aqueduct links the third to the fourth ventricle. Obstruction causes CSF to accumulate upstream in the third and lateral ventricles.
questions.distractor_note: The fourth ventricle lies downstream of the aqueduct and is not the primary site of enlargement in an isolated aqueduct blockage.
questions.dropped_distractor: The lateral ventricles and fourth ventricle only

questions.stem: Mean arterial pressure is 95 mmHg and intracranial pressure is 15 mmHg. Assuming cerebral venous pressure is not higher than intracranial pressure, what is cerebral perfusion pressure?
options: 65 mmHg
75 mmHg
80 mmHg
95 mmHg
questions.explanation: Cerebral perfusion pressure is approximately MAP - ICP when ICP is the effective downstream pressure: 95 - 15 = 80 mmHg.
questions.distractor_note: Perfusion pressure is a difference between driving and downstream pressures; it is not the MAP alone.
questions.dropped_distractor: 110 mmHg

questions.stem: Why does most left ventricular coronary blood flow occur during diastole rather than systole?
options: The left coronary artery is closed by the aortic valve during systole.
The heart stops using oxygen during systole.
Pulmonary venous pressure becomes higher than aortic pressure during systole.
Contracting left ventricular muscle compresses vessels within its wall.
questions.explanation: During left ventricular systole, high intramyocardial pressure compresses coronary vessels, especially in the subendocardium. Relaxation during diastole permits better perfusion.
questions.distractor_note: Coronary arterial openings remain connected to the aorta; the critical factor is compression by contracting myocardium.
questions.dropped_distractor: Blood in coronary arteries contains oxygen only during diastole.

questions.stem: One group of alveoli is poorly ventilated while nearby alveoli are well ventilated. What happens to the small pulmonary arteries supplying the poorly ventilated region?
options: They dilate, directing more blood toward the poorly ventilated alveoli.
They remain unchanged because oxygen never affects pulmonary resistance.
They constrict only if systemic arterial pressure is also high.
They constrict, directing more blood toward better-ventilated alveoli.
questions.explanation: Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary arteriolar constriction. This helps divert flow toward alveoli where oxygen uptake is more effective.
questions.distractor_note: The pulmonary hypoxic response is opposite to the usual local hypoxic vasodilation in systemic tissues.
questions.dropped_distractor: They close because all pulmonary arteries normally lack smooth muscle.

questions.stem: During exercise, pulmonary blood flow increases greatly but pulmonary arterial pressure rises relatively little. What helps explain this?
options: Most pulmonary capillaries close as flow increases.
Previously underperfused capillaries open and existing vessels widen.
Pulmonary vascular resistance increases in direct proportion to flow.
The alveoli stop exchanging gases while blood flow rises.
questions.explanation: Recruitment of additional pulmonary capillaries and distension of vessels increase the total flow capacity, limiting the rise in pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure.
questions.distractor_note: Recruitment and distension expand, not reduce, pulmonary vascular capacity.
questions.dropped_distractor: The right ventricle stops pumping blood during exercise.

questions.stem: After firm stroking of the skin, redness spreads beyond the directly stimulated line. What produces this surrounding flare?
options: An axon reflex causing nearby arterioles to dilate
Clotting of capillaries at the site of injury
Closure of all precapillary sphincters around the area
Direct filtration of red blood cells into the epidermis
questions.explanation: The flare of the triple response is produced by an antidromic axon reflex that dilates vessels around the stimulated region.
questions.distractor_note: The wheal reflects increased local permeability, whereas the flare is spreading arteriolar vasodilation.
questions.dropped_distractor: A sudden fall in total circulating blood volume

questions.stem: What change occurs in the pulmonary circulation with the newborn's first breaths?
options: Pulmonary vascular resistance rises as alveolar oxygen rises.
Pulmonary vascular resistance falls as the lungs expand and oxygen rises.
The ductus venosus begins carrying blood from the right ventricle.
Systemic vascular resistance falls because the placenta remains connected.
questions.explanation: Lung expansion and increased alveolar oxygen reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, raising pulmonary blood flow. Loss of the placenta simultaneously tends to raise systemic vascular resistance.
questions.distractor_note: The first breaths promote pulmonary vasodilation, not vasoconstriction.
questions.dropped_distractor: Pulmonary blood flow stops because placental blood flow has ended.

questions.section: 2. Why can the tracing move upwards or downwards?
questions.stem: In a lead where the QRS is upright, the T wave is often upright too. Which combined explanation best accounts for this?
options: Repolarisation has the same electrical sign and travels in the same direction through the ventricles.
Repolarisation has opposite polarity and generally travels in the reverse direction.
Repolarisation has opposite polarity but travels in the same direction.
Repolarisation has the same polarity but travels in the reverse direction.
questions.explanation: A repolarisation wave has the opposite electrical sign to depolarisation; ventricular repolarisation also progresses in the reverse order, producing a T wave often concordant with QRS.
distractors: Depolarisation and repolarisation do not have the same electrical polarity.
Opposite polarity without reversed direction would favour opposite QRS/T deflections.
Reversed direction without the polarity reversal would also favour opposite deflections.

questions.stem: At 25 mm/s, consecutive ECG R waves are separated by 20 small horizontal squares. What is the ventricular rate?
options: 60 beats/min
75 beats/min
80 beats/min
100 beats/min
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, one small square = 0.04 s. Twenty squares = 0.8 s per beat, giving 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min. Equivalently, 1500/20 = 75 beats/min.
questions.distractor_note: Heart rate depends on the R-R interval; the standard 25 mm/s conversion yields 1500 divided by small squares.
questions.dropped_distractor: 120 beats/min

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.section: 4. Why are the a, c and v waves separated by x and y descents?
questions.stem: What distinguishes the normal x descent from the y descent in a JVP trace?
options: x: atrial relaxation; y: emptying through the open tricuspid.
x: atrial contraction; y: ventricular isovolumetric contraction.
x: ventricular ejection; y: pulmonary arterial recoil.
x: aortic valve opening; y: mitral valve closure.
questions.explanation: The x descent reflects atrial relaxation and downward tricuspid movement; the y descent follows tricuspid opening as blood empties rapidly.
distractors: Atrial contraction creates the a wave.
Both descents reflect right atrial pressure changes rather than the proposed events.
Left-heart valve events do not define these JVP descents.

questions.stem: Why might severe anaemia produce a cardiac flow murmur despite structurally normal valves?
options: Lower viscosity and increased flow favour turbulence.
Reduced blood volume necessarily closes the aortic valve.
Anaemia markedly increases blood viscosity and suppresses flow.
Anaemia blocks the ventricular conduction system.
questions.explanation: Anaemia lowers viscosity and may increase cardiac output, raising the tendency to turbulent flow and a functional murmur.
distractors: The murmur is not due to forced aortic valve closure.
Anaemia decreases viscosity rather than increasing it.
Conduction block is not the principal mechanism of flow murmurs.

questions.section: 2. Intercalated discs: how separate cells function together
questions.stem: How can an impulse spread rapidly between adjacent cardiac muscle cells?
options: Gap junctions provide low-resistance electrical connections.
Each cell must first receive a motor-neuron endplate signal.
The connective tissue between cells conducts sodium current.
Mechanical desmosomes independently generate pacemaker signals.
questions.explanation: Gap junctions in intercalated discs permit ion current to spread from cell to cell, supporting a functional syncytium.
distractors: Cardiac muscle does not require motor endplates for every contraction.
Connective tissue does not replace electrically coupled membranes.
Desmosomes provide mechanical attachment rather than electrical conductance.

questions.section: 2. The control centre in the medulla
questions.stem: Damage selectively removes the inhibitory effect of the medullary depressor area on the pressor area. Which response is expected?
options: Reduced local metabolism with fixed arteriolar diameter.
Greater sympathetic discharge with increased vascular tone.
Greater vagal discharge with isolated venous dilation.
Reduced sympathetic discharge with markedly decreased vascular tone.
questions.explanation: The depressor area normally inhibits the pressor area; removing this brake permits more sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity.
distractors: Local tissue metabolism is not directly abolished by this lesion.
A selective loss of pressor inhibition does not primarily increase vagal output.
Disinhibition would increase, not decrease, pressor drive.

questions.section: 5. Chemoreceptors
questions.stem: A patient has low arterial oxygen and high carbon dioxide. Which peripheral sensors respond mainly to these chemical changes?
options: The atrial type A and type B volume receptors.
The carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors.
The sinoatrial and atrioventricular pacemaker nodes.
The carotid bodies and the aortic bodies.
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies monitor oxygen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions, chiefly stimulating breathing.
distractors: Atrial volume receptors principally detect filling and stretch.
Arterial baroreceptors principally detect stretch.
Cardiac nodes generate and conduct impulses rather than monitor arterial chemistry.

questions.section: 7. Other inputs, and the lecture’s “exceptions”
questions.stem: Inflation of the lungs sends sensory impulses towards the medulla. What cardiovascular response is described in the lecture?
options: Atrial volume-receptor excitation with sustained vasoconstriction.
Carotid sinus chemoreceptor inhibition with increased arterial tone.
Sympathetic afferent excitation of vasomotor activity with constriction.
Vagal afferent inhibition of vasomotor activity with vasodilation.
questions.explanation: The lecture states that lung-inflation afferents travel in the vagus and can inhibit the vasomotor centre, lowering vascular tone and pressure.
distractors: This is a lung-inflation input rather than an atrial filling response.
The carotid sinus is a stretch receptor, and the described effect is dilation.
The named afferent pathway is vagal and its effect is depressor.

questions.section: 4. How the body fights back
questions.stem: After bleeding stops, both haemoglobin and plasma-protein concentrations fall as circulating volume recovers. What explains this?
options: Added fluid dilutes the remaining blood components.
New red-cell production lowers haemoglobin concentration.
Raised renal filtration removes most circulating proteins.
Venoconstriction selectively removes haemoglobin from blood.
questions.explanation: Fluid recruited from tissues or given intravenously restores volume before red-cell and protein mass recover, producing dilution.
distractors: New red-cell production raises rather than lowers haemoglobin mass.
Renal filtration is generally depressed during acute severe shock.
Venoconstriction redistributes blood rather than removing haemoglobin.

questions.section: 4. When compensation fails: prolonged standing and fainting
questions.stem: An older patient faints shortly after standing to urinate at night. Which phenomenon does this episode most closely illustrate?
options: Carotid sinus syncope caused by neck pressure.
Micturition syncope linked to reflex hypotension.
Septic shock due to widespread inflammatory vasodilatation.
Positive-g blackout from head-level underperfusion.
questions.explanation: Micturition syncope is fainting associated with urination, often after rising at night, due to a reflex pressure fall.
distractors: Carotid sinus syncope requires stimulation of a sensitive carotid region.
There is no evidence of infection-related shock in the stem.
Normal standing to urinate is not high positive acceleration.

questions.stem: A patient has near-normal resting cardiac output but very high ventricular filling pressures and pulmonary congestion. Which statement fits best?
options: Heart failure can occur with normal output.
High filling pressure proves adequate pumping.
Heart failure requires reduced ejection fraction.
Normal resting output excludes heart failure.
questions.explanation: Heart failure includes states where output is maintained only at abnormally high filling pressures, causing congestion.
distractors: High filling pressures can be evidence of dysfunction rather than normality.
Diastolic failure can occur with preserved ejection fraction.
A near-normal output can be maintained at harmful filling pressures.

questions.section: 4. What does the body do about it, and why does that make it worse?
questions.stem: Why can prolonged renin–angiotensin–aldosterone activation worsen heart-failure oedema?
options: It causes sustained urinary sodium loss.
It decreases circulating volume and filling pressure.
Salt and water retention raises venous pressure.
It prevents compensatory arterial vasoconstriction.
questions.explanation: RAAS initially supports blood pressure, but prolonged salt and water retention increases filling pressures and oedema.
distractors: Aldosterone promotes sodium retention rather than loss.
RAAS tends to expand, not deplete, extracellular volume.
Angiotensin II supports rather than blocks vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: Portal hypertension promotes ascites partly by increasing which force?
options: Plasma oncotic pressure within hepatic capillaries.
Hydrostatic pressure in hepatic sinusoids.
Interstitial lymphatic pumping efficiency.
Arterial oxygen tension in the hepatic vein.
questions.explanation: Higher sinusoidal hydrostatic pressure increases fluid filtration and hepatic lymph formation; excess can enter the peritoneal cavity.
distractors: Higher plasma oncotic pressure would oppose outward fluid filtration.
Improved lymphatic clearance would tend to oppose accumulation.
Oxygen tension is not the main Starling-force mechanism.

questions.chapter: Chapter 27 — Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth
questions.stem: Why does fetal haemoglobin load oxygen effectively at the placental interface?
options: It binds 2,3-BPG more tightly than adult haemoglobin.
Its weaker 2,3-BPG binding increases oxygen affinity.
It is produced without haem groups before birth.
Its iron permanently binds each oxygen molecule.
questions.explanation: HbF interacts less with 2,3-BPG, shifting its oxygen dissociation curve left and favouring oxygen uptake from maternal blood.
distractors: Stronger 2,3-BPG binding would lower oxygen affinity.
Fetal haemoglobin still contains iron-bearing haem groups.
Oxygen binding is reversible, not permanent.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 5. The coverings, the ventricles and CSF
questions.stem: A patient develops headache that is worse upright after lumbar CSF sampling. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Persistent CSF leakage lowers intracranial CSF pressure.
The sample immediately increases blood–brain barrier permeability.
Lumbar puncture increases CSF production several-fold.
The procedure obstructs both foramina of Monro.
questions.explanation: Leakage from the dural puncture can reduce CSF pressure and cause a characteristic postural headache.
distractors: BBB disruption is not the usual cause of post-lumbar-puncture headache.
Production does not normally surge to cause this symptom.
The foramina are far from the lumbar puncture site.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 6. The blood–brain barrier
questions.stem: Which structure forms the key physical restriction to paracellular movement across the blood–brain barrier?
options: Astrocytic end-feet alone.
The choroid plexus epithelium.
Loose junctions of cerebral venules.
Endothelial tight junctions.
questions.explanation: Tight junctions in cerebral capillary endothelium restrict movement between cells; astrocytes support barrier function.
distractors: Astrocytes help maintain the barrier but are not the main sealed endothelial layer.
The choroid plexus forms a separate blood–CSF barrier.
Loose venular junctions would not account for selective restriction.

questions.section: 4. Waves, segments and intervals: what is the difference?
questions.stem: An ECG develops a new shift of the ST segment above or below the baseline. Which process specifically makes this segment clinically important?
options: Myocardial ischaemia or inadequate oxygenation can alter ST level.
Normal atrial depolarisation creates the ST deflection of each beat.
A decrease in cardiac preload directly determines ST segment height.
The onset of valve closure normally lifts the ST segment above baseline.
questions.explanation: Ventricular ischaemia or hypoxia can disturb membrane potentials and cause ST elevation or depression, so the segment is useful in recognising myocardial injury patterns.
distractors: Atrial depolarisation is the P wave and normally precedes ST.
Preload is a filling variable and does not directly set ST height.
ST displacement is an electrical finding, not the normal marker of valve closure.

questions.stem: At 25 mm/s, a PR interval extends across 4.5 small squares. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: 0.24 s, above the stated PR-interval range.
0.09 s, shorter than the stated normal PR-interval range.
0.90 s, above the stated PR-interval range.
0.18 s, inside the stated PR-interval range.
questions.explanation: The horizontal duration is 4.5 × 0.04 = 0.18 s. This lies within the 0.12–0.20 s interval given in the lecture.
distractors: This is not the product of 4.5 and 0.04 s.
This incorrectly halves the duration obtained from 4.5 small squares.
This incorrectly assigns 0.20 s to each small square.

questions.section: 3. Why can ten electrodes produce twelve ECG leads?
questions.stem: Why is aVF classed as an augmented unipolar limb lead?
options: It compares two fixed chest electrodes in the horizontal plane of the heart.
It uses the left-foot electrode against an averaged limb reference.
It compares the right arm directly against the left arm.
It uses the right-leg electrode as its positive terminal.
questions.explanation: In aVF the left-foot electrode is positive and is compared with an average reference derived from the two arm electrodes.
distractors: Chest electrodes make up V1–V6 and mainly examine the horizontal plane.
Right arm versus left arm describes bipolar Lead I.
The right-leg electrode is used for electrical noise reduction.

questions.section: 4. Waves, segments and intervals: what is the difference?
questions.stem: Why is the normal T wave generally broader than the QRS complex?
options: The T wave covers atrial and ventricular depolarisation together.
Ventricular depolarisation spreads more slowly than repolarisation.
The T wave corresponds to ventricular contraction rather than electricity.
Ventricular repolarisation usually takes longer than its depolarisation.
questions.explanation: The T wave reflects the slower process of ventricular repolarisation, while QRS represents rapid ventricular depolarisation through the conduction system.
distractors: Atrial and ventricular depolarisation are represented mainly by P and QRS.
The statement reverses the usual relative time courses.
The T wave is still an electrical event, not the force of contraction.

questions.section: 8. Basic rhythm assessment (supplementary)
questions.stem: Which feature most reliably distinguishes first-degree AV block from second-degree AV block in the chapter’s basic ECG classification?
options: Both have identical PR intervals on each beat.
Both show independent P-wave and QRS rhythms.
First-degree conducts every P; second-degree drops some.
First-degree lacks P waves; second-degree lacks QRS complexes.
questions.explanation: First-degree block delays conduction but retains a QRS after every P wave. In second-degree block, at least some atrial impulses fail to produce QRS complexes.
distractors: Second-degree block is defined by intermittent failed conduction, not identical PR intervals.
Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms indicate complete third-degree block.
Both conditions can show P waves and QRS complexes on the trace.

questions.section: 1. What does an ECG actually record?
questions.stem: Two beats have different QRS heights. A student concludes the taller complex produced a larger stroke volume. What is the main flaw?
options: QRS height represents the duration of ventricular contraction.
QRS height directly records the pressure within the ventricle.
QRS height measures the amount of venous blood returning.
QRS height reflects voltage, not the amount of blood ejected.
questions.explanation: The ECG measures electrical potentials. A larger recorded deflection may reflect electrical orientation or amplitude; it does not directly quantify mechanical stroke volume.
distractors: Duration is measured horizontally on ECG paper, not from complex height.
A surface ECG records electrical potential rather than ventricular pressure.
Venous return is a haemodynamic variable not directly measured by the tracing.

questions.chapter: Chapter 26 — Cutaneous Circulation and the Triple Response
questions.section: 2. Skin blood flow in shock
questions.stem: A patient in compensated haemorrhagic shock has cold, pale skin. Which mechanism accounts for this?
options: Increased sympathetic cutaneous vasoconstriction.
Loss of vasomotor drive causing widespread dilation.
Increased skin capillary blood volume from vasodilation.
Direct activation of warm-sensitive skin receptors.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic constriction reduces skin flow to preserve perfusion for vital organs, producing pallor and coolness.
distractors: Loss of sympathetic tone would usually warm and flush skin.
Higher cutaneous blood volume tends to increase redness.
The primary response is systemic compensation, not skin warming.

questions.stem: Which pressure relationship helps prevent fluid accumulation in normal pulmonary alveoli?
options: Pulmonary capillary pressure consistently exceeds systemic arterial pressure.
Absence of plasma proteins in pulmonary capillaries.
Relatively low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.
Higher alveolar protein pressure than in capillary plasma.
questions.explanation: Low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure relative to plasma oncotic forces helps minimise filtration into air spaces.
distractors: Pulmonary capillary pressure is much lower than systemic arterial pressure.
Plasma proteins contribute the inward oncotic force.
Alveolar spaces normally contain little free fluid and protein.

questions.stem: A cuff that is far too small is used on a large upper arm. Which measurement error is likely?
options: No systematic effect on cuff pressure.
An undersized cuff gives a falsely high reading.
Only diastolic pressure becomes unmeasurable.
Falsely low BP from excessive arterial unloading.
questions.explanation: An undersized cuff transmits pressure poorly around a large arm and commonly overestimates measured pressure.
distractors: Cuff size materially affects readings.
Both systolic and diastolic measurements may be distorted.
A small cuff usually overestimates rather than underestimates BP.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.stem: The CSF volume is about 150 mL and production is 550 mL/day. Approximately how many complete turnovers occur per day?
options: About 4.
About 2.
About 1.
About 6.
questions.explanation: Dividing daily production by total CSF volume gives 550/150 ≈ 3.7 turnovers each day.
distractors: Two turnovers would require about 300 mL/day.
One turnover would represent only about 150 mL/day.
Six turnovers would correspond to around 900 mL/day.

questions.stem: Increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure while other Starling forces stay unchanged tends to produce what?
options: Decreased outward fluid filtration.
More fluid filtration into tissues.
Reversal of lymphatic flow.
Increased plasma oncotic attraction.
questions.explanation: A higher capillary hydrostatic force favours filtration across the microvascular wall toward tissue. Raising venous pressure is one way to produce this hydrostatic change.
distractors: The pressure favours outward, not reduced, filtration.
Lymphatic flow generally responds to excess tissue fluid rather than reversing.
Plasma oncotic pressure does not automatically increase.

questions.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
questions.stem: A patient develops cardiac tamponade. Why can stroke volume fall despite a normal blood volume?
options: Tamponade increases functional ventricular compliance.
Tamponade directly raises venous return above normal.
The aortic valve cannot open due solely to a high heart rate.
High pericardial pressure restricts ventricular filling.
questions.explanation: Elevated intrapericardial pressure limits end-diastolic filling and preload, reducing stroke volume. The restricted ventricular volume prevents an adequate Frank–Starling response.
distractors: Tamponade reduces the ability of ventricles to expand.
Venous return and effective filling become impaired.
Valvular opening depends on pressure, but reduced preload is the central problem.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: Arterial pressure inside an arteriole is unchanged, but pressure in its surrounding tissue rises. What happens to transmural pressure?
options: It decreases because the pressure difference narrows.
It increases because the pressure difference widens.
It becomes identical to intravascular arterial pressure.
It remains fixed because arterial pressure is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Transmural pressure equals internal pressure minus surrounding tissue pressure; increasing the latter reduces the difference.
distractors: A higher external pressure reduces, rather than widens, the difference.
It equals internal pressure only when external pressure is zero.
Transmural pressure depends on both internal and external pressure.

questions.stem: A severely underperfused patient begins breathing rapidly, although the lungs were initially healthy. What drives this change?
options: Increased aerobic ATP production stimulates breathing.
Suppression of the peripheral chemoreceptors stimulates breathing.
Lactic acidosis stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.
High tissue oxygen content increases respiratory drive.
questions.explanation: Inadequate tissue oxygen delivery promotes anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis. The resulting acidemia can stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors and increase ventilation; reduced oxygen delivery alone is not equivalent to low arterial oxygen tension.
distractors: Aerobic metabolism is limited by inadequate oxygen delivery.
Chemoreceptor stimulation, rather than suppression, promotes respiration.
Excess oxygen is not the initiating problem in shock.

questions.stem: How does local hypoxia affect most systemic arterioles versus pulmonary arterioles?
options: Systemic vessels constrict while pulmonary vessels dilate.
Both primarily constrict to lower oxygen delivery.
Both remain relatively insensitive to tissue oxygen.
Systemic vessels dilate; pulmonary vessels constrict.
questions.explanation: Systemic hypoxic tissues commonly dilate to improve supply, whereas low alveolar oxygen constricts adjacent pulmonary arterioles to improve ventilation–perfusion matching.
distractors: The response directions have been reversed.
Systemic tissues usually need increased flow in hypoxia.
Oxygen tension influences both beds, but their dominant local responses differ.

questions.stem: A pressure tracing shows atrial contraction shortly after an ECG P wave and ventricular contraction shortly after QRS. What principle explains both delays?
options: Electrical excitation normally precedes the mechanical response of cardiac muscle.
Mechanical contraction normally finishes before electrical activation begins in the chamber.
The T wave must occur before either chamber can begin contraction.
Atrial and ventricular pressures directly create the corresponding ECG waves.
questions.explanation: The electrical depolarisation that activates cardiac muscle precedes its force development. P precedes atrial systole, and QRS precedes ventricular systole.
distractors: This reverses the normal electrical-to-mechanical sequence.
The T wave reflects ventricular electrical recovery, after ventricular depolarisation.
Pressure changes follow electrical activation and are not what skin ECG leads measure.

questions.stem: What extra perspective do the chest leads V1–V6 add to the standard limb-lead views?
options: They replace voltage measurement with intracardiac pressure.
They remove the need to record the frontal electrical plane.
They isolate atrial electrical activity from ventricular activity.
They show cardiac electrical vectors in the horizontal plane.
questions.explanation: The limb leads provide frontal-plane views, while the precordial leads examine the same heart from different points around the horizontal plane.
distractors: Chest leads, like limb leads, still record surface electrical potentials.
Frontal and horizontal views complement rather than replace one another.
Both sets of leads record combined cardiac electrical events.

questions.stem: During progressive shock, capillary hydrostatic pressure paradoxically rises while systemic arterial pressure is falling. Which microvascular pattern best explains it?
options: Precapillary constriction with freely draining venules.
Increased venular drainage with reduced capillary entry.
Open capillary entry with constricted venules.
Precapillary constriction with widened venous outlets.
questions.explanation: With capillary entry relatively open but venular outflow restricted, blood stagnates and local capillary pressure rises, driving fluid into the interstitium.
distractors: Lower entry with free outflow would not cause the described stasis.
Greater drainage would reduce rather than increase local stagnation.
Both reduced entry and improved drainage favour lower capillary pressure.

questions.stem: Lead II has an upright QRS while aVR has a downward QRS during the same beat. What best explains the difference?
options: Each lead projects the same electrical vector onto a different axis.
One lead measures depolarisation and the other repolarisation.
The two leads record different mechanical contractions.
Atrial and ventricular activity alternate between the leads on each beat.
questions.explanation: A lead is a directional electrical view. The normal mean ventricular depolarisation vector points generally towards Lead II and away from aVR.
distractors: Both QRS complexes represent ventricular depolarisation, despite opposite polarity.
Both leads sample the electrical activity of the same heartbeat.
Lead orientation does not change the sequence of atrial and ventricular activation.

questions.stem: A patient with marked polycythaemia has elevated haematocrit. What is the expected direct effect on systemic flow resistance?
options: Lower viscosity and lower total vascular resistance.
Higher viscosity and lower resistance.
Higher viscosity and higher resistance.
Lower viscosity and higher resistance.
questions.explanation: More red cells increase blood viscosity and consequently vascular resistance, raising the heart's workload.
distractors: Both properties generally increase, not decrease.
Higher viscosity raises resistance rather than lowering it.
Lower viscosity does not follow from higher haematocrit.

questions.section: 1. Why does the body need central control?
questions.stem: Cardiac output falls by 20%, but total peripheral resistance rises by 25%. What happens to mean arterial pressure in the simplified MAP relation?
options: It remains approximately unchanged.
It decreases by approximately one quarter.
It increases by approximately one quarter.
It decreases by approximately one fifth.
questions.explanation: In MAP ≈ CO × TPR, 0.80 × 1.25 = 1.00, so the changes cancel mathematically.
distractors: The combined product does not fall by one quarter.
That ignores the fall in cardiac output.
That ignores the compensatory rise in resistance.

questions.stem: At one instant, Lead I records +0.4 mV and Lead III records −0.2 mV. What must Lead II record?
options: −0.2 mV, from using the third lead alone.
+0.6 mV, from adding their magnitudes.
+0.2 mV, from adding the signed voltages.
−0.6 mV, from subtracting the two values.
questions.explanation: Einthoven’s law is V(II) = V(I) + V(III). Therefore +0.4 + (−0.2) = +0.2 mV at the same instant.
distractors: Lead II is obtained by combining the two measured limb-lead voltages.
The negative sign of Lead III must be retained in the sum.
This reverses the sign of the result rather than adding the signed voltages.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: A region of heart muscle starts working harder. Which local product of its own metabolism helps increase its blood flow?
options: Serotonin released by nearby platelets.
Angiotensin II formed in the blood.
Noradrenaline from sympathetic nerves.
Adenosine formed as ATP is used up.
questions.explanation: Working muscle uses ATP faster, and its breakdown products (adenosine, ADP, AMP) build up and dilate the local arterioles. Flow rises in proportion to how hard the tissue works, which is why the heart relies so heavily on this.
distractors: Platelet serotonin constricts vessels, and it comes from platelets, not from the working muscle.
Angiotensin II is a circulating constrictor, not a product of the muscle’s metabolism.
Noradrenaline is a nerve transmitter that mainly constricts arterioles via α₁ receptors.

questions.stem: What physiological purpose is served by slow conduction through the AV node?
options: It prevents the impulse from ever reaching the ventricular myocardium.
It ensures ventricles eject before the atria contract.
It allows the aortic valve to remain open during atrial systole.
It allows atrial contraction to finish ventricular filling.
questions.explanation: The AV delay separates atrial and ventricular activation so atrial systole can augment ventricular filling before ventricular systole.
distractors: Normal impulses subsequently travel through His and Purkinje fibres.
The sequence is atrial activation before ventricular activation.
The aortic valve remains closed during ordinary atrial systole.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the updated interpretation of capillary fluid balance?
options: The glycocalyx regulates filtration; lymph returns excess fluid.
Lymphatic vessels play no role when hydrostatic pressure is normal.
Most capillaries continuously reabsorb nearly all filtered fluid at their venous ends.
Interstitial proteins do not affect exchange at any capillary.
questions.explanation: The revised Starling model includes the glycocalyx and emphasises that sustained net filtration is normally cleared by lymphatics.
distractors: Lymphatic return remains vital even at normal pressures.
The classical arterial filtration–venous reabsorption picture overstates sustained reabsorption.
Protein distributions can influence effective oncotic gradients.

questions.stem: Minutes after a severe allergic exposure, a patient's pressure drops with generalised swelling. Which vascular action is most relevant?
options: Histamine-related dilatation with increased capillary permeability.
Generalised constriction with reduced capillary permeability.
Increased myocardial pump function with reduced venous capacitance.
Selective haemorrhage into the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis releases mediators including histamine that widen vessels and increase capillary leakage, reducing effective perfusion.
distractors: Anaphylaxis typically causes dilation and increased leak.
Higher pump performance would not explain the sudden widespread leakage.
Occult bleeding is not the primary allergic vascular mechanism.

questions.stem: How does normal inspiration tend to assist systemic venous return?
options: It increases right atrial pressure and reduces abdominal pressure.
It closes all systemic venous valves simultaneously.
It increases peripheral venous capacitance until return stops.
Lower chest pressure draws venous blood toward the heart.
questions.explanation: Inspiration decreases intrathoracic pressure and promotes a pressure gradient drawing blood from peripheral veins to the thorax.
distractors: Lower rather than higher thoracic pressure assists inflow.
Venous valves do not all close in inspiration.
Return is generally supported rather than abolished.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: An exercising leg receives increased blood flow while its muscle continues contracting. What is this response called?
options: Active hyperaemia driven by ongoing tissue metabolism.
Reactive hyperaemia following a temporary flow block.
Baroreflex vasodilation after systemic arterial pressure rises.
Autoregulation that holds its flow at rest level.
questions.explanation: Active hyperaemia is the rise in flow while a tissue is working: its metabolites dilate the arterioles for as long as activity continues. Reactive hyperaemia is the surge after a blockage is released.
distractors: Reactive hyperaemia is a surge after an obstruction ends.
The increase originates largely from local demand, not a pressure-rise baroreflex.
The flow rises above baseline rather than staying constant.

questions.section: 5. Orthostatic (postural) hypotension
questions.stem: After three minutes upright, pressure changes from 126/82 to 104/77 mmHg. How is this classified using the chapter criterion?
options: No orthostatic hypotension because diastolic pressure fell only 5 mmHg.
No orthostatic hypotension because final systolic pressure exceeds 100 mmHg.
Orthostatic hypotension because systolic pressure fell 22 mmHg.
Orthostatic hypotension only if both pressures fall by 20 mmHg.
questions.explanation: A sustained systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg within three minutes satisfies the criterion.
distractors: The systolic threshold is met even when the diastolic threshold is not.
The diagnostic threshold concerns the change, not a fixed final pressure.
The definition does not require both components to fall by 20 mmHg.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.section: 3. Two mechanisms: myogenic and metabolic
questions.stem: Two cylindrical vessels have equal transmural pressure, but vessel X has twice the radius of vessel Y. How do their required wall tensions compare?
options: Both vessels require exactly the same wall tension.
Vessel X requires half the wall tension of Y.
Vessel X requires four times the tension of Y.
Vessel X requires twice the wall tension of Y.
questions.explanation: For a cylinder, wall tension T = P × r. With equal transmural pressure, the vessel with twice the radius needs twice the tension. This is why a capillary’s tiny radius lets a one-cell wall withstand blood pressure.
distractors: Equal pressure alone does not make tension equal.
Half the tension would apply to half the radius.
A fourfold difference does not follow the linear radius relation.

questions.section: 6. How do ECG paper squares represent time and voltage?
questions.stem: An ECG is repeated at 50 mm/s instead of 25 mm/s, with no change in the patient's conduction. How does the same 0.16-s PR interval appear?
options: It occupies half as many horizontal squares as on the slower recording.
It occupies twice the former number of horizontal squares.
It occupies the same number of horizontal squares.
It occupies twice the former number of vertical squares.
questions.explanation: Doubling paper speed doubles the horizontal distance covered during a fixed physiological interval. A 0.16-s PR interval spans 8 mm at 50 mm/s versus 4 mm at 25 mm/s.
distractors: A faster recording speed spreads the same time over more paper, not less.
The number of squares changes because time calibration depends on paper speed.
Vertical squares measure voltage and are unaffected by horizontal paper speed.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 6. The blood–brain barrier
questions.stem: Brain glucose uptake remains adequate despite an intact blood-brain barrier that restricts passage between endothelial cells. What transport process explains this?
options: By free movement through tight junctions.
Through a specific endothelial transporter.
Through bulk passage of plasma proteins.
Through insulin-triggered endothelial pores.
questions.explanation: Glucose crosses the BBB through transporters such as GLUT1; its entry does not require insulin.
distractors: Endothelial tight junctions block most paracellular solutes.
Protein leakage is limited by the barrier.
Cerebral glucose transport is largely insulin independent.

questions.section: 4. Excitation–contraction coupling: from electrical signal to force
questions.stem: How does calcium entering through L-type channels activate a much larger ventricular calcium signal?
options: It directly hydrolyses ATP within actin.
It triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
It causes SERCA to release its stored calcium outward.
It closes ryanodine receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
questions.explanation: Trigger calcium opens ryanodine receptors, releasing stored calcium in calcium-induced calcium release. This amplifies the small trigger signal into a large intracellular calcium release.
distractors: Calcium binds troponin C; ATP hydrolysis occurs in cross-bridge cycling.
SERCA pumps calcium back into the SR during relaxation.
Ryanodine receptors open rather than close in this mechanism.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 3. How does the brain keep its blood flow steady?
questions.stem: A highly active cortical region accumulates carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions. What is the expected local vascular response?
options: Local arterioles constrict, reducing perfusion.
Local arterioles dilate, increasing perfusion.
Capillaries close while arteriolar tone stays fixed.
Venules constrict without an arteriolar response.
questions.explanation: Increased local CO₂ and H⁺ cause cerebral arteriolar vasodilation, improving blood delivery to metabolically active tissue.
distractors: Constriction would reduce flow to the region that needs more oxygen.
Capillary closure would worsen rather than correct the local supply-demand mismatch.
Isolated venular constriction does not explain metabolic regulation of cerebral arteriolar inflow.

questions.section: 8. Basic rhythm assessment (supplementary)
questions.stem: Regular P waves continue at one rate and QRS complexes at a slower independent rate, with no fixed PR relationship. Which rhythm disturbance is present?
options: Sinus rhythm with a normal PR interval.
First-degree atrioventricular block.
Second-degree atrioventricular block.
Third-degree atrioventricular block.
questions.explanation: Complete (third-degree) block produces atrioventricular dissociation: atria and ventricles follow independent rhythms without consistent P-to-QRS conduction.
distractors: Normal sinus rhythm has a consistent P wave preceding each conducted QRS.
First-degree block maintains a consistent P-to-QRS relationship with prolonged PR.
Second-degree block has intermittent failure, rather than complete independence.

questions.stem: A patient with massive haemorrhage remains severely hypotensive after blood volume is completely restored. Which stage fits?
options: Early compensated hypovolaemic shock with intact reflexes.
Irreversible shock after extensive tissue injury.
Postural hypotension from remaining upright.
Transient vasovagal faint without major tissue damage.
questions.explanation: Severe myocardial, neural and microvascular damage may prevent recovery even after the original blood-volume loss has been corrected.
distractors: Compensated shock should retain useful mechanisms for pressure support.
Postural hypotension should depend on standing and impaired compensation.
An uncomplicated faint generally improves rapidly when lying flat.

questions.stem: A bleeding patient has a nearly normal arterial pressure but cold skin and reduced urine output. What is the best conclusion?
options: Normal pressure excludes significant shock.
Low perfusion can coexist with normal pressure.
Cardiac output must be above its pre-bleeding level.
Blood flow to all organs must remain normal.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic arteriolar constriction can maintain arterial pressure despite reduced cardiac output and poor perfusion of some tissues.
distractors: Shock is defined by inadequate tissue perfusion, not one pressure value.
Haemorrhage reduces venous return and usually lowers output.
Flow can be redistributed away from skin and kidneys.

questions.stem: Why can chronic widespread alveolar hypoxia lead to pulmonary hypertension?
options: Persistent hypoxia opens every pulmonary capillary without resistance.
Persistent hypoxic constriction increases lung resistance.
Widespread hypoxia lowers pulmonary vascular smooth-muscle tone.
Chronic hypoxia eliminates blood passing through the lungs.
questions.explanation: When hypoxic constriction affects much of the lung, cumulative resistance rises and pulmonary arterial pressure can increase.
distractors: Recruitment is a different response that lowers resistance.
The lecture explicitly associates hypoxia with pulmonary vasoconstriction.
Lung flow generally continues but faces increased resistance.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: Once local metabolic dilation restores an organ’s blood flow, what prevents dilation from continuing unchecked?
options: The restored flow removes oxygen from the tissue cells.
The restored flow causes a sustained rise in local lactate.
The restored flow clears accumulated dilator metabolites.
The restored flow abolishes vessel-wall smooth muscle.
questions.explanation: The dilators exist because flow was too low for demand. Once flow matches demand, they are washed away as fast as they are made, so the arterioles regain their tone. This negative feedback stops dilation running away.
distractors: Restored delivery generally improves tissue oxygen availability.
Sustained lactate accumulation would favour continued dilation.
Vascular smooth muscle remains present and functional.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: A graph of organ flow against perfusion pressure is almost flat over a middle range but slopes downward at very low pressures. Why?
options: The arterioles reach their maximal dilation at low pressure.
The arterioles reach their maximal constriction at low pressure.
The heart stops driving any pressure into the organ.
The veins become the principal resistance at low pressure.
questions.explanation: Once arterioles are fully dilated, they cannot reduce resistance further, so flow decreases as pressure falls.
distractors: Maximal constriction occurs in response to rising pressure, not very low pressure.
A downward slope does not mean perfusion pressure is zero.
Venous vessels do not replace arterioles as the chief resistance site.

questions.stem: A burn patient presents with shock and an initially high haematocrit. What explains the contrast with recent whole-blood haemorrhage?
options: Burns selectively destroy red cells circulating in blood.
Burns produce increased circulating volume despite shock.
Burns cause immediate erythropoietin-driven erythrocytosis.
Plasma leakage leaves intravascular red cells concentrated.
questions.explanation: Severe burns can cause plasma to leak through damaged skin while red cells remain, producing haemoconcentration and raised haematocrit.
distractors: Selective red-cell destruction would tend to lower red-cell concentration.
Plasma loss reduces rather than increases effective circulating volume.
Erythropoiesis is much too slow to explain this early result.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.stem: The jugular venous 'c' wave is chiefly linked to which event?
options: Rapid emptying of the right atrium.
Passive systemic venous filling late in systole.
Systolic bulging of the tricuspid valve.
Right atrial contraction immediately before QRS.
questions.explanation: Early right ventricular contraction can bulge the shut tricuspid valve toward the right atrium, contributing to the c wave.
distractors: Rapid atrial emptying contributes to the y descent.
Venous filling behind a closed tricuspid valve makes the v wave.
Right atrial systole generates the a wave.

questions.section: 5. Ejection: why blood finally leaves
questions.stem: In a normal cardiac cycle, how does the rate of ventricular ejection change after the semilunar valves open?
options: It starts rapidly and then becomes reduced ejection.
It starts slowly and accelerates until valve closure.
It remains identical in flow throughout systole.
It begins only after ventricular relaxation.
questions.explanation: The ejection phase has an initial rapid phase followed by reduced ejection as the pressure and flow relationship changes.
distractors: The pattern is the reverse of the usual ejection phases.
Ejection rate declines rather than remaining uniform.
Ejection occurs during ventricular systole, before relaxation.

questions.section: 4. What causes S3 and S4?
questions.stem: What produces an S4 in a patient with a stiff ventricle?
options: Opening of the pulmonary valve against high pressure.
Rapid early-diastolic filling before any atrial activity.
Atrial contraction into a poorly compliant ventricle.
Turbulence during systolic outflow across a normal aortic valve.
questions.explanation: S4 is associated with late-diastolic atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, which causes low-frequency vibrations.
distractors: Pulmonary valve opening occurs in systole.
Rapid passive filling is associated with S3 rather than S4.
Systolic ejection turbulence describes a murmur, not S4.

questions.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
questions.section: 2. Why can changing heart rate alter cardiac output?
questions.stem: Why might increasing heart rate far above normal eventually reduce cardiac output?
options: Contractility necessarily falls to zero.
Diastolic time becomes longer and increases filling.
The mitral valve is forced to remain permanently open.
Shorter diastole reduces filling and stroke volume.
questions.explanation: Extreme tachycardia shortens diastole, reduces filling and may decrease stroke volume enough to lower output.
distractors: Contractility does not necessarily become zero.
Diastole shortens markedly at high rates.
Normal valves do not remain permanently open during extreme tachycardia.

questions.section: 3. The cardiac muscle action potential
questions.stem: A ventricular action potential has a prolonged plateau. Which membrane currents chiefly sustain it?
options: Rapid sodium entry alone throughout the entire plateau.
Increased potassium efflux without any inward current.
Calcium inflow balanced by outward potassium current.
Absence of calcium entry with continued chloride influx.
questions.explanation: Slow inward calcium current and outward potassium current maintain the prolonged plateau before repolarisation.
distractors: Fast sodium influx creates phase 0, not the sustained plateau.
Unopposed potassium efflux would favour repolarisation.
Calcium entry contributes substantially to phase 2.

questions.section: 5. Why can low plasma proteins cause oedema?
questions.stem: Why may advanced liver disease cause generalised oedema even without venous obstruction?
options: Excess albumin synthesis draws water into tissues.
Less albumin synthesis reduces plasma oncotic pressure.
A rise in plasma protein concentration stops absorption.
Liver failure directly shuts every lymphatic valve.
questions.explanation: Reduced albumin production lowers intravascular colloid oncotic pressure, allowing more net filtration and oedema.
distractors: Advanced liver disease commonly reduces albumin synthesis.
Plasma protein concentration is decreased, not increased.
Lymphatic valve closure is not the universal mechanism.

questions.stem: A harsh systolic murmur develops during blood ejection through a narrowed aortic valve. What mechanism explains it?
options: Opening of the aortic valve during ventricular relaxation.
Turbulent forward flow through a stenotic outflow orifice.
Regurgitation through the mitral valve during diastole.
Laminar blood flow through a normal-sized valve.
questions.explanation: Aortic stenosis accelerates blood through a narrow outlet during systole, causing a turbulent ejection murmur.
distractors: The aortic valve opens when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure in systole.
Mitral regurgitation usually occurs during systole, not diastole.
Laminar flow through normal valves ordinarily produces no such murmur.

questions.stem: Which pressure difference primarily drives blood back to the right atrium from the body?
options: Aortic systolic minus right ventricular systolic pressure.
Left ventricular systolic minus aortic diastolic pressure.
Systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure.
Pulmonary venous minus pulmonary capillary pressure.
questions.explanation: Venous return depends on the upstream systemic filling pressure relative to right atrial pressure and the resistance to venous return.
distractors: Aortic-right ventricular systolic pressure is not the venous return driving gradient.
That difference is a pulse-pressure-related comparison.
Pulmonary venous pressure does not define systemic venous return.

questions.stem: At an otherwise unchanged capillary, how would increased interstitial protein concentration affect fluid movement?
options: It increases protein attraction into the blood compartment.
It strengthens plasma oncotic pressure, reducing filtration.
It lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure, opposing filtration.
It strengthens the outward oncotic force favouring filtration.
questions.explanation: More interstitial protein increases interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, tending to pull fluid outward from the capillary and increase filtration.
distractors: Increased proteins outside the capillary attract rather than remove interstitial water.
Plasma protein concentration is held constant; the changed force is interstitial.
A change in interstitial protein does not directly lower capillary pressure.

questions.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
questions.section: 9. What happens to cardiac output during exercise and other states?
questions.stem: During graded exercise, which combination helps increase cardiac output?
options: Greater vagal activity and smaller stroke volume.
