Reduced sympathetic drive and greater afterload.
Slower pacemaking and lower venous return.
Higher rate, contractility and venous return.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic drive raises heart rate and contractility while muscle pumping supports venous return, enabling higher cardiac output.
distractors: Vagal dominance would tend to slow the heart.
Reduced sympathetic drive does not explain exercise output.
Exercise generally increases rather than suppresses cardiac pumping.

questions.chapter: Chapter 8 — Measuring Cardiac Output and the Work of the Heart
questions.section: 5. What does it mean for the heart to perform work?
questions.stem: What does the mechanical stroke work of a ventricle represent?
options: Electrical energy in the SA node over one minute.
The number of coronary capillaries recruited.
Heart rate multiplied by body surface area.
Ventricular pressure–volume work per beat.
questions.explanation: The ventricle performs pressure–volume work as it ejects stroke volume against an arterial pressure load.
distractors: Pacemaker electrical energy is not mechanical stroke work.
Capillary recruitment affects supply, not the definition of work.
Heart rate and surface area do not directly define mechanical work.

questions.section: 5. Laminar flow, turbulence and Reynolds number
questions.stem: For steady laminar flow through a straight tube, where is linear velocity highest?
options: At the endothelial wall.
At the vessel centre.
Uniformly across the lumen.
At the outer plasma layer.
questions.explanation: Viscous drag slows flow near the wall; a parabolic velocity profile has its greatest velocity near the centre.
distractors: The no-slip boundary makes velocity near the wall approach zero.
Laminar flow has a radial velocity gradient.
The plasma layer adjacent to the wall is not the maximum-velocity region.

questions.section: 5. Why is the intestinal lymphatic system important in fat absorption?
questions.stem: After a meal containing long-chain fats, which pathway carries these lipids from the gut?
options: Direct red-cell delivery to lacteals.
Renal filtration of absorbed fats.
Oxygenated blood flow through the portal vein alone.
Chylomicron transport from intestinal lacteals.
questions.explanation: Absorbed long-chain fats are packaged into chylomicrons and enter lacteals, reaching the blood via lymphatic drainage.
distractors: Red cells normally remain in blood vessels.
Kidneys do not mediate initial intestinal fat absorption.
Most long-chain dietary fat reaches systemic blood through lymph rather than directly through portal blood.

questions.stem: Heart rate rises from 70 to 80 beats/min while stroke volume stays at 70 mL. By how much does cardiac output increase?
options: By 0.80 litres per minute.
By 0.70 litres per minute.
By about 0.49 litres per minute.
By 1.40 litres per minute.
questions.explanation: The increase is 10 beats/min × 70 mL/beat = 700 mL/min, or 0.70 L/min.
distractors: 0.80 L/min treats the extra beats as a larger volume.
0.49 L/min does not follow from the given rate change.
1.40 L/min doubles the actual change.

questions.section: 3. The baroreflex, step by step
questions.stem: A haemorrhage suddenly lowers blood pressure. Which changes help restore it through the arterial baroreflex?
options: Increased sympathetic drive and reduced vagal drive.
Reduced sympathetic drive and greater venous storage.
Reduced sympathetic drive and increased vagal drive.
Increased vagal drive and reduced venous return.
questions.explanation: Lower afferent firing releases the pressor area and reduces vagal inhibition, raising heart rate, contractility and vascular tone.
distractors: Sympathetic withdrawal and venous storage would further lower pressure.
That combination is appropriate to a rise in pressure.
Greater vagal drive would slow the heart, while low return worsens output.

questions.section: 4. Control of the heart: sympathetic and vagus
questions.stem: An isolated SA node fires at about 100 beats/min, whereas the same person’s resting pulse was about 70. Which interpretation best fits?
options: Atrial conduction had slowed the spontaneous SA nodal rate.
The cardiac pacemaker was intrinsically limited to 70.
Resting vagal activity had restrained SA nodal firing.
Resting sympathetic activity had restrained SA nodal firing.
questions.explanation: With no nerve input the SA node fires at about 100 beats/min. At rest the vagus releases acetylcholine continuously (vagal tone), holding the rate down to about 60–80. Blocking the vagus, for example with atropine, lets the rate rise.
distractors: Atrial conduction is not the main cause of the slower intrinsic SA pacemaker rate.
The isolated rate shows the pacemaker is capable of firing faster.
Sympathetic activity usually increases SA nodal firing.

questions.stem: A patient has low circulating volume. Which hormone chiefly increases renal water retention and can constrict vessels at high concentration?
options: Vasopressin, also called ADH.
Atrial natriuretic peptide.
Vasoactive intestinal peptide.
Endothelial prostacyclin.
questions.explanation: ADH promotes renal water conservation and has a vasoconstrictor action when its level is high.
distractors: ANP promotes sodium and water loss.
VIP is a vasodilator rather than a water-retaining hormone.
Prostacyclin dilates vessels and limits platelet aggregation.

questions.stem: Which contrast best distinguishes forward failure from backward failure?
options: Forward reduces delivery; backward causes venous congestion.
Forward is venous congestion; backward is low organ blood flow.
Forward indicates excess cardiac output; backward low afterload.
Forward is confined to the right heart; backward to the left.
questions.explanation: Forward failure describes inadequate delivery to downstream tissues, whereas backward failure describes elevated pressure and congestion upstream of a failing chamber.
distractors: The two effects are reversed in this statement.
Reduced flow and congestion, not excessive output, are the defining patterns.
Either side can produce both forward and backward consequences.

questions.stem: An examination reveals raised JVP, a tender enlarged liver, ascites and ankle oedema. Which haemodynamic change unifies these?
options: High systemic venous pressure behind the right ventricle.
Reduced filtration from peripheral capillaries.
Increased pulmonary venous pressure without systemic congestion.
Reduced central venous pressure from depleted blood volume.
questions.explanation: Right ventricular backward failure elevates right atrial and systemic venous pressures, causing jugular distension, hepatic congestion and dependent oedema.
distractors: Higher systemic venous pressure promotes, rather than reduces, filtration.
Isolated pulmonary venous congestion principally reflects left-sided failure.
Right-sided backward failure increases rather than decreases venous pressure.

questions.stem: A patient with left-sided forward heart failure reports fatigue and produces very little urine. Which mechanism links the two?
options: Elevated venous pressure increases renal filtration.
Reduced systemic perfusion limits muscle and renal blood flow.
Pulmonary congestion causes systemic arteriolar dilation.
Increased left ventricular output stimulates renal water loss.
questions.explanation: Reduced blood ejected from the left heart impairs delivery to skeletal muscle and kidneys, causing fatigue and oliguria.
distractors: Higher venous pressure does not directly improve GFR.
The primary forward mechanism is reduced output, not pulmonary congestion.
The syndrome involves reduced rather than excessive systemic delivery.

questions.stem: During severe hepatic hypoperfusion, cells near the central vein are especially vulnerable to hypoxia. Why?
options: They are located outside the hepatic sinusoidal network.
They are closest to arterial inflow.
They are farthest downstream from the portal triads.
They receive blood with the highest oxygen content.
questions.explanation: Centrilobular cells receive blood after it has travelled from portal triads, making them less oxygenated and vulnerable.
distractors: Centrilobular hepatocytes remain within the sinusoidal perfusion system.
Oxygenated hepatic arterial inflow enters near the portal triads.
Blood oxygen content generally falls as it traverses sinusoids.

questions.chapter: Chapter 27 — Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth
questions.stem: Why does the fetal cardiovascular system divert much blood away from the pulmonary circuit before birth?
options: The fetal left ventricle cannot generate arterial pressure.
Pulmonary vascular resistance is exceptionally low before birth.
Umbilical arteries carry already oxygenated blood to the heart.
The placenta oxygenates blood; fetal lungs resist flow.
questions.explanation: The placenta performs gas exchange before birth; fluid-filled fetal lungs have high resistance, favouring right-to-left shunts.
distractors: The fetal left ventricle contributes significantly to systemic output.
Pulmonary resistance is high before aeration.
Umbilical arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood toward placenta.

questions.section: 5. Why can tachycardia cause ischaemia?
questions.stem: Why is a patient with significant coronary narrowing more vulnerable to angina when heart rate rises sharply?
options: The P wave disappears and blocks blood flow.
Myocardial oxygen consumption falls below baseline.
The coronary sinus develops arterial hypertension.
Shorter diastole and higher myocardial demand.
questions.explanation: Tachycardia increases cardiac oxygen demand and shortens diastole, reducing the time available for left ventricular coronary perfusion.
distractors: An absent P wave is not the explanation of demand-related angina.
Myocardial work and oxygen consumption generally rise with tachycardia.
The primary limitation is coronary supply through stenosed arteries during shortened diastole.

questions.stem: A technician places V1 at the fourth intercostal space. Where should the electrode be positioned horizontally?
options: At the left midclavicular line.
At the anterior axillary line.
At the right sternal border.
At the left midaxillary line.
questions.explanation: V1 is positioned in the fourth intercostal space at the right edge of the sternum; V2 lies at the left sternal edge at the same level.
distractors: The left midclavicular line in the fifth space is the usual site of V4.
The anterior axillary position is used for V5.
The midaxillary position is used for V6.

questions.section: 4. Waves, segments and intervals: what is the difference?
questions.stem: The ST segment is nearly flat despite an actively contracting ventricle. What electrical state best explains that appearance?
options: The ventricle has completed repolarisation and returns to electrical rest.
Most ventricular cells are depolarised together in their plateau phase.
The atria and ventricles are depolarising in opposite directions.
The AV node is holding all impulses before ventricular activation.
questions.explanation: With much of the ventricular myocardium at a similar depolarised membrane potential during the plateau, there is little net voltage difference to register.
distractors: Ventricular repolarisation occurs during the following T wave, not before ST.
Atrial and ventricular opposing depolarisations do not account for normal ST isoelectricity.
By ST, the impulse has already activated the ventricles.

questions.section: 4. Waves, segments and intervals: what is the difference?
questions.stem: A student calls the entire PR interval “the AV nodal delay.” What important part of the interval does this description miss?
options: The time between the end of QRS and the start of T.
The period during which the ventricular myocardium is repolarising.
The delay between ventricular systole and valve opening.
The spread through atria and conduction towards the ventricles.
questions.explanation: PR includes the P wave itself and conduction through atrial tissue, AV node and His–Purkinje system before QRS begins. AV nodal delay is only one component.
distractors: End-QRS to start-T corresponds to the ST segment.
Ventricular repolarisation is represented by T and included in QT.
Mechanical valve events are not boundaries of the PR interval.

questions.stem: Which response becomes particularly important for supporting pressure during sustained rather than momentary upright posture?
options: Renin–angiotensin effects and renal salt retention.
Suppression of aldosterone-driven sodium retention.
Persistent inhibition of all vascular reflexes.
Loss of sympathetic arteriolar responsiveness.
questions.explanation: The rapid baroreflex stabilizes pressure within seconds, while the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system supports longer-term pressure and volume.
distractors: Aldosterone supports sodium retention rather than its suppression.
Baroreflexes remain available during sustained standing.
Loss of arteriolar responsiveness would worsen orthostatic control.

questions.stem: A person becomes angry during an argument, and both pulse and pressure rise. Which route can initiate this response?
options: Cortical signals acting through the hypothalamus on autonomic centres.
Atrial filling signals acting through the kidneys on increased urine output.
Cerebral CSF signals acting through the ventricles on the heart.
Platelet serotonin acting through capillaries on cardiac pacing.
questions.explanation: Emotions such as anger begin in the cortex. The cortex drives the hypothalamus, which excites the vasomotor centre, raising sympathetic output so heart rate and blood pressure rise.
distractors: Renal volume control is too slow and not the primary emotional route.
The CSF pathways do not directly account for this autonomic response.
Platelet serotonin is a local vascular constrictor, not the main emotional signal.

questions.stem: Why can vision fail before consciousness during strong positive acceleration?
options: Retinal perfusion falls as blood shifts toward the feet.
The retina receives blood at higher pressure than the heart.
Intracranial pressure exceeds local arterial pressure.
Positive acceleration shifts blood toward the head.
questions.explanation: Positive g causes leg pooling and reduced pressure at eye level, so retinal perfusion can fail before cerebral consciousness.
distractors: Pressure at eye level decreases during positive g.
The mechanism is reduced eye-level arterial perfusion, not an inevitable ICP excess.
Headward blood movement occurs during negative g.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly characterises isovolumetric ventricular contraction?
options: All valves closed, ventricular pressure rises, volume fixed.
AV valves open, semilunar valves open, volume rises.
AV valves open, semilunar valves shut, volume falls.
All valves closed, ventricular pressure falls, volume fixed.
questions.explanation: Both ventricles generate rising pressure with all inlet and outlet valves closed, so neither receives nor ejects blood.
distractors: Open valves permit volume exchange.
AV valves do not remain open once ventricular pressure rises above atrial.
Falling pressure describes isovolumetric relaxation, not contraction.

questions.stem: A patient loses substantial albumin into urine during kidney disease. What Starling-force change is expected?
options: Increased red-cell viscosity causing filtration.
Reduced capillary permeability everywhere.
Increased plasma colloid osmotic pressure.
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure promotes oedema.
questions.explanation: Proteinuria reduces circulating albumin and its inward oncotic force, favouring movement of fluid into interstitium.
distractors: Viscosity is not the principal mechanism of protein-loss oedema.
Capillary permeability elsewhere need not decrease.
Albumin loss lowers oncotic pressure.

questions.section: 4. How does coronary flow match changing myocardial work?
questions.stem: Cardiac beta-adrenergic stimulation raises coronary flow overall mainly through which chain?
options: Less contraction → less oxygen use → greater vascular tone.
More contraction → less ATP use → less adenosine.
More work → metabolites → arteriolar dilation.
Direct beta stimulation → closure of coronary arterioles.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation raises cardiac work and oxygen demand; local metabolites then increase coronary perfusion despite competing vasomotor effects.
distractors: Reduced contraction is not the expected beta-mediated cardiac response.
Greater work increases, not reduces, ATP consumption.
Coronary flow is not increased by closing the arterioles.

questions.stem: Beta-1 adrenergic stimulation generally increases ventricular contractility through which sequence?
options: Blocked ryanodine receptors → larger systolic calcium release.
Increased cAMP/PKA signalling → greater calcium availability.
Increased vagal tone → reduced pacemaker slope → stronger contraction.
Reduced cAMP → less calcium entry → weaker contraction.
questions.explanation: Beta-1 signalling raises cAMP and PKA activity, enhancing calcium entry and cycling for stronger contraction.
distractors: Blocking release channels would reduce systolic calcium release.
Vagal slowing is not the main ventricular inotropic pathway.
Beta-1 stimulation raises, not lowers, cAMP.

questions.section: 2. Systolic and diastolic failure: can't squeeze, or can't fill?
questions.stem: A stiff ventricle has high filling pressure but a preserved ejection fraction. What is the primary defect?
options: Impaired relaxation and filling.
Increased contractility and ejection.
Reduced electrical activation of the SA node.
Excessive ventricular compliance.
questions.explanation: Diastolic failure reflects impaired relaxation and stiff ventricular filling; the fraction of blood ejected can remain normal despite elevated filling pressures and reduced filling volume.
distractors: Increased contractility is not the primary defect.
SA-node dysfunction does not define diastolic heart failure.
A stiff ventricle has reduced, not excessive, compliance.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.section: 6. Local control and the whole body
questions.stem: During exercise, sympathetic activity increases throughout the body, yet working muscle receives much more blood. Which explanation is best?
options: A higher systemic pressure redirects flow equally among tissues.
Systemic arteriolar constriction raises every tissue’s flow equally.
Local metabolic dilation outweighs constriction in active muscle.
Local metabolic constriction outweighs dilation in active muscle.
questions.explanation: Active muscle generates enough vasodilator metabolites to oppose sympathetic constriction, redirecting blood to the tissue that needs it.
distractors: Sympathetic activity often remains elevated; metabolites oppose its constrictor effect locally.
Constriction does not raise flow equally across every organ.
Metabolites in working muscle predominantly dilate its arterioles.

questions.stem: A standard ECG uses ten skin electrodes but produces twelve electrical views. How is this possible?
options: Two extra electrodes inside the heart are automatically activated for recording.
Several leads are calculated from combinations of the same electrode voltages.
Each electrode produces one lead, with two more produced by blood-pressure sensors.
The limb electrodes are relocated to the chest during every cardiac cycle.
questions.explanation: A lead is an electrical viewpoint calculated from one or more electrode potentials, so ten physical contacts can generate twelve different standard recordings.
distractors: Routine twelve-lead ECG does not require intracardiac electrodes.
All twelve are electrical leads; pressure sensors do not generate extra leads.
The limb contacts remain in place during a standard recording.

questions.stem: Why does positioning an accelerating pilot more horizontally improve tolerance to positive g?
options: It shortens the heart-to-brain hydrostatic column.
It increases the distance between the heart and brain.
It directs pooled blood toward the ankles.
It raises the capillary filtration rate in the legs.
questions.explanation: A more horizontal posture decreases the vertical distance over which acceleration reduces pressure toward the head and brain.
distractors: Increasing the vertical distance would worsen the gradient.
Enhanced ankle pooling would reduce central venous return.
Greater dependent filtration would not protect brain perfusion.

questions.stem: A ventricular depolarisation vector runs almost perpendicular to the viewing axis of a lead. What should that lead record?
options: A small or biphasic ventricular deflection.
A tall downward ventricular deflection.
A tall upright ventricular deflection.
A prolonged ventricular depolarisation interval.
questions.explanation: Only the component of the electrical vector along the lead axis contributes strongly to the deflection; a near-perpendicular vector has a small projection.
distractors: A strongly downward deflection needs a substantial vector component away from the positive pole.
A strongly upright deflection needs a substantial vector component towards the positive pole.
Vector orientation changes amplitude and polarity, not necessarily conduction duration.

questions.chapter: Chapter 8 — Measuring Cardiac Output and the Work of the Heart
questions.section: 3. Where do the oxygen measurements come from?
questions.stem: In a whole-body Fick measurement, which blood should the return-side oxygen sample represent?
options: Oxygenated blood in a systemic artery.
Mixed venous blood entering the lungs.
Blood in a single peripheral venule.
Capillary blood from active skeletal muscle only.
questions.explanation: A mixed venous sample from pulmonary artery reflects oxygen after extraction across the whole body.
distractors: Arterial blood provides the other concentration in the equation.
One local vein does not represent average whole-body extraction.
Active muscle has unusually high local extraction and can misrepresent the body.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.section: 7. Which abnormal JVP waves are most important?
questions.stem: A patient with severe tricuspid regurgitation has a prominent systolic jugular venous wave. Which wave becomes especially large?
options: a wave.
v wave.
x descent.
y descent.
questions.explanation: Tricuspid regurgitation sends systolic flow back into the right atrium and systemic veins, producing a large v or fused c-v wave.
distractors: The a wave reflects atrial contraction and is not the characteristic regurgitant finding.
The x descent may be blunted rather than unusually enlarged.
The y descent is an emptying phase and does not represent systolic backflow.

questions.stem: During standing, head-level arterial pressure falls by 30 mmHg and cerebral venous pressure falls by 25 mmHg. How does arterial minus venous driving pressure change?
options: It falls by about 25 mmHg.
It rises by about 5 mmHg.
It falls by about 5 mmHg.
It rises by about 55 mmHg.
questions.explanation: The arterial–venous difference changes by −30 minus −25, or −5 mmHg. Falling venous and intracranial pressures therefore help protect cerebral perfusion.
distractors: That ignores the fall in cerebral venous pressure.
The difference becomes slightly smaller, not larger.
The changes cannot be added as two rises.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 6. The blood–brain barrier
questions.stem: Which substance passes relatively readily across the intact blood–brain barrier without a carrier?
options: Plasma albumin.
A protein-bound drug.
Carbon dioxide.
A large immunoglobulin.
questions.explanation: Small diffusible gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the endothelial membrane relatively easily.
distractors: Albumin is a large protein with restricted passage.
Protein binding reduces free diffusion across the BBB.
Large immunoglobulins do not easily cross intact endothelial tight junctions.

questions.section: 5. When shock feeds on itself: progressive and irreversible shock
questions.stem: How can impaired coronary perfusion create a vicious cycle during severe shock?
options: Coronary ischaemia weakens contraction, further reducing output.
Low coronary blood flow increases myocardial ATP stores.
Myocardial hypoxia lowers arterial resistance enough to compensate.
Reduced stroke volume directly increases coronary perfusion pressure.
questions.explanation: Coronary ischaemia depresses myocardial contractility, lowering output and pressure, which further compromises myocardial blood supply.
distractors: Ischaemia reduces rather than increases available myocardial ATP.
Lower resistance cannot fully resolve a collapsing pump.
Lower cardiac output tends to worsen coronary perfusion, not restore it.

questions.stem: A low-frequency third heart sound occurs in early diastole. What ventricular event coincides with it?
options: Atrial depolarisation before systole.
Isovolumetric ventricular contraction.
Rapid passive ventricular filling.
Opening of the aortic valve.
questions.explanation: S3 occurs during rapid early-diastolic ventricular filling, as blood entering the chamber causes vibrations.
distractors: Atrial depolarisation precedes the atrial contribution later in diastole.
Isovolumetric contraction occurs near S1.
Aortic valve opening occurs during ventricular systole.

questions.stem: A small additional deflection appears after the T wave in an otherwise interpretable trace. Which description fits the U wave?
options: Atrial depolarisation occurring before the next P wave.
A possible late ventricular repolarisation phenomenon.
Rapid ventricular depolarisation immediately before QRS.
A ventricular plateau interval between QRS and T.
questions.explanation: The lecture describes a U wave, when seen after T, as the final remnants of ventricular repolarisation. Its precise physiological origin is uncertain.
distractors: Atrial depolarisation is the P wave preceding QRS.
Rapid ventricular depolarisation is represented by QRS, not U.
The ventricular plateau is associated with the ST segment.

questions.chapter: Chapter 26 — Cutaneous Circulation and the Triple Response
questions.section: 1. Skin blood flow is mainly about heat, not nutrition
questions.stem: What role do arteriovenous anastomoses serve in fingers and other exposed skin?
options: They transfer blood directly into lymphatic capillaries.
They prevent sympathetic regulation of skin perfusion.
They permanently close when environmental temperature rises.
They provide adjustable shunts for heat exchange.
questions.explanation: AV anastomoses can vary cutaneous blood delivery and heat transfer according to thermoregulatory needs.
distractors: They connect arteries and veins rather than blood to lymph.
Skin shunts are under autonomic control.
Their opening and closing vary with temperature regulation.

questions.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
questions.section: 7. What changes contractility?
questions.stem: Why can xanthines such as theophylline produce a positive inotropic effect at the signalling level described in the lecture?
options: They reduce the breakdown of intracellular cAMP.
They directly prevent L-type calcium-channel opening.
They accelerate the breakdown of intracellular cAMP.
They permanently suppress myocardial beta-1 receptors.
questions.explanation: The lecture describes phosphodiesterase inhibition by xanthines, which slows cAMP breakdown; increased cAMP-dependent signalling can enhance myocardial calcium handling and contractility.
distractors: Reducing calcium entry would tend to depress rather than enhance contraction.
Faster cAMP degradation would reduce this positive inotropic pathway.
Blocking beta-1 signalling would generally reduce adrenergic inotropy.

questions.stem: Why is a distinct atrial repolarisation wave usually absent from a normal ECG?
options: Atrial repolarisation generates no electrical voltage differences.
The atria cannot repolarise until ventricular diastole begins.
Its small electrical signal is obscured by the ventricular QRS complex.
Atrial repolarisation occurs just before the SA node starts the next beat.
questions.explanation: Atrial repolarisation occurs around the time of ventricular depolarisation; the much larger QRS electrical signal masks it on the surface trace.
distractors: Repolarisation does generate voltage differences, although the signal is small.
Atrial repolarisation does not need to await the beginning of ventricular diastole.
That statement does not explain why the wave is not separately visible.

questions.stem: A measured QRS occupies 3.5 small squares at 25 mm/s. Which statement is supported by the lecture’s usual duration range?
options: It lasts 0.10 s and is at the upper edge of the stated range.
It lasts 0.14 s and is longer than the stated usual range.
It lasts 0.07 s and is within the stated usual range.
It lasts 0.35 s and is longer than the stated usual range.
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, 3.5 small squares equal 3.5 × 0.04 = 0.14 s, above the lecture’s usual QRS duration of 0.06–0.10 s.
distractors: 0.10 s corresponds to 2.5 small squares at the standard speed.
0.07 s incorrectly halves the 0.14-s measured duration.
0.35 s does not follow from the standard 0.04-s small-square duration.

questions.stem: A patient becomes dizzy on standing after starting a sympatholytic drug. Which compensatory response is most directly weakened?
options: Contraction of calf muscles during walking.
Flow of blood through competent venous valves.
Dilatation of cerebral vessels by carbon dioxide.
Constriction of systemic arterioles and veins.
questions.explanation: Sympatholytic drugs blunt reflex arteriolar and venous constriction, so the circulation cannot adequately oppose blood pooling and falling arterial pressure on standing.
distractors: Walking uses a mechanical muscle pump, not this autonomic drug pathway.
Venous valve directionality is mechanical and not directly abolished by sympatholytic drugs.
Cerebral metabolic vasodilatation is not directly a sympathetic vasoconstrictor response.

questions.section: 1. Why does the body need central control?
questions.stem: A drug primarily dilates large systemic veins rather than arterioles. Which immediate circulatory change is most likely?
options: More blood is stored in the venous reservoir.
Peripheral resistance rises sharply in the arterioles.
Capillary smooth-muscle contraction becomes stronger.
More blood is forced towards the right atrium.
questions.explanation: Venodilation increases capacitance, allowing veins to hold more blood and tending to reduce venous return.
distractors: Arteriolar tone is the principal determinant of peripheral resistance.
Capillaries are not the main contractile vessels.
Venoconstriction, not venodilation, mobilises stored blood.

questions.stem: What closes the aortic valve at the beginning of ventricular relaxation?
options: Venous pressure exceeds aortic pressure.
Atrial pressure rises above left ventricular pressure.
Aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure.
Left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure.
questions.explanation: When ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, brief reversal tendency closes the aortic valve and starts isovolumetric relaxation.
distractors: Venous pressure does not directly determine aortic valve closure.
Atrial pressure governs mitral opening, not aortic closure.
Ventricular pressure exceeding aortic pressure opens the valve.

questions.chapter: Chapter 27 — Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth
questions.section: 4. What closes after delivery?
questions.stem: After cord clamping and lung aeration, what pressure change favours functional closure of the foramen ovale?
options: Right atrial pressure rises above left atrial pressure.
Pulmonary resistance remains very high.
Umbilical venous inflow increases right atrial pressure.
Left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure.
questions.explanation: Increased pulmonary venous return elevates left atrial pressure while loss of placental venous return reduces right-sided filling, pressing the flap closed.
distractors: Right atrial dominance normally supports fetal shunting, not closure.
Pulmonary resistance falls with first breaths.
Clamping removes rather than increases umbilical venous return.

questions.stem: A patient has had high arterial pressure for months. Why might baroreceptors fail to drive pressure back to the original baseline?
options: Their operating range resets around the sustained level.
Their stretch sensitivity increases indefinitely without adaptation.
Their afferent pathways turn into motor pathways over time.
Their signals stop entering the medulla during hypertension.
questions.explanation: When pressure stays high for days, the baroreceptors reset and treat the new level as normal, so they defend it instead of correcting it. Long-term pressure is set mainly by the kidneys’ control of salt and water.
distractors: Unbounded sensitivity would strongly oppose the persistent rise.
Sensory fibres do not become motor fibres.
Resetting does not require loss of every afferent signal.

questions.chapter: Chapter 26 — Cutaneous Circulation and the Triple Response
questions.stem: A very light stroke briefly leaves a pale line on the skin. How is this reaction best classified?
options: The wheal component of the triple response.
The red line of local capillary dilation.
The spread of an axon-reflex flare.
A brief local vasoconstrictor response.
questions.explanation: The lecture describes a transient white reaction due to constriction; it is distinct from the classical red–flare–wheal response.
distractors: Wheal is raised local oedema from permeability.
The red line is a separate vasodilator response.
Flare is surrounding redness from arteriolar dilation.

questions.stem: How can fluid enter a blind-ended lymphatic capillary when interstitial pressure rises?
options: A continuous layer of smooth muscle forces plasma outward.
A central lymphatic heart pumps blood into tissues.
Rigid endothelial junctions prevent all protein entry.
Overlapping endothelial flaps admit interstitial fluid.
questions.explanation: Initial lymphatic endothelial flaps allow interstitial fluid and proteins to enter when surrounding pressure exceeds lymphatic pressure.
distractors: Initial lymphatic capillaries lack a thick continuous smooth-muscle coat.
There is no single central lymphatic heart.
Initial lymphatics are relatively permeable to interstitial proteins.

questions.section: 8. Clinical significance of conduction disturbances
questions.stem: A ventricular impulse occurs independently of atrial excitation after complete AV conduction block. What has happened?
options: The SA node has increased its firing rate.
The aortic valves transmit an alternate impulse.
Atrial excitation now travels directly through the lungs.
A subsidiary escape pacemaker has taken over.
questions.explanation: Complete AV block prevents atrial impulses from reaching ventricles; a slower escape pacemaker may maintain ventricular rhythm.
distractors: Faster atrial activity alone cannot restore complete AV conduction.
Valves do not propagate cardiac electrical impulses.
The lungs do not provide an alternative physiological conduction path.

questions.stem: A patient with raised intracranial pressure develops hypertension and bradycardia together. What best explains the slow pulse?
options: The hypertension directly activates cardiac beta-1 receptors.
The cardiac pacemaker stops responding to vagal signals.
The arterial baroreflex reacts to the sympathetic pressure rise.
The atrial volume reflex reacts to the sympathetic pressure rise.
questions.explanation: Medullary ischaemia first raises sympathetic pressure; arterial baroreceptors then increase vagal drive and slow the heart.
distractors: β₁ stimulation would usually accelerate, not slow, the heart.
Cardiac autonomic signalling remains central to the response.
Atrial volume receptors respond chiefly to filling, not this sequence.

questions.section: 7. Other inputs, and the lecture’s “exceptions”
questions.stem: A brief sharp pain raises a patient’s pressure, but prolonged severe pain later causes faintness. What best accounts for the difference?
options: A brief pressor phase gives way to vasodilation.
Early venous pooling gives way to strong vasoconstriction.
Long pain increases total peripheral resistance without limit.
Brief pain reduces sympathetic output from central pathways.
questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes the pressor response to short, sharp pain from depressor vasodilation and possible syncope with sustained pain.
distractors: The directions of vascular changes are reversed in this option.
Prolonged pain may produce hypotension rather than unbounded resistance.
Short sharp pain can stimulate rather than inhibit pressor activity.

questions.section: 6. Why is ventricular conduction so rapid?
questions.stem: Why do Purkinje fibres help the two ventricles contract as coordinated pumps?
options: They slow excitation until the pulmonary valve closes.
They rapidly activate ventricular myocardium.
They delay the impulse longer than the AV node does.
They selectively depolarise only the atrial septum.
questions.explanation: Rapid His–Purkinje conduction activates much of ventricular myocardium in a short time for synchronised pumping.
distractors: Pulmonary valve closure occurs after ventricular ejection.
The key AV delay occurs before the His–Purkinje network.
Purkinje fibres primarily serve ventricles, not the atrial septum.

questions.stem: Arterial pressure increases suddenly and baroreceptor firing rises. What changes first in central reflex control?
options: NTS activation increases depressor and vagal signalling.
The SA node starts generating impulses without modulation.
NTS activation increases pressor and spinal sympathetic firing.
Sensory traffic to the medulla decreases despite added stretch.
questions.explanation: More stretch → faster baroreceptor firing → more input to the NTS. The NTS excites the depressor area (which inhibits the pressor area) and the vagal neurons, so sympathetic output falls and vagal output rises.
distractors: The heart remains under autonomic regulation during the reflex.
The reflex suppresses rather than increases sympathetic pressor drive.
Increased wall stretch increases, rather than decreases, afferent traffic.

questions.stem: A sudden increase in sympathetic venous tone can support cardiac output mainly through which immediate effect?
options: It closes arteriolar valves and stops peripheral outflow.
It dilates veins, increasing blood stored in the limbs.
It creates new circulating plasma within seconds.
Venoconstriction shifts stored blood centrally.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic venoconstriction reduces the capacity of the venous reservoir and shifts stored blood toward the heart, supporting venous return and end-diastolic filling.
distractors: Systemic arterioles have no valves that close with sympathetic stimulation.
Venodilation generally increases peripheral capacitance and pooling.
Venoconstriction redistributes existing blood rather than rapidly generating plasma.

questions.stem: What most clearly differentiates myocardial infarction from brief stable angina?
options: Prolonged ischaemia can produce myocyte necrosis.
Infarction occurs only when heart rate is very slow.
Angina permanently destroys the affected myocardium.
Angina requires complete coronary artery rupture.
questions.explanation: Prolonged severe ischaemia can cause irreversible myocardial cell death; transient angina does not necessarily cause necrosis.
distractors: Infarction can occur across a range of heart rates.
Transient angina ordinarily reflects reversible myocardial ischaemia.
Stable angina may result from fixed stenosis without rupture.

questions.stem: What helps maintain forward systemic arterial flow between heartbeats?
options: Venous valves directly generate aortic pressure.
The elastic recoil of large arteries sustains diastolic flow.
The diaphragm pumps blood through the aorta during inspiration.
Capillaries generate contractions that propel blood upstream.
questions.explanation: Elastic arteries stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing pulsatile ejection into continuous downstream flow.
distractors: Venous valves prevent backflow but do not create aortic pressure.
Respiratory movement mainly assists venous return.
Capillaries lack the pumping muscle required to drive systemic flow.

questions.stem: A patient with coronary atheroma is comfortable at rest but develops exertional chest pain. Which explanation fits best?
options: The coronary artery becomes completely normal during exercise.
Restricted coronary flow reserve cannot meet increased demand.
Exercise lowers heart oxygen requirements below resting levels.
Coronary flow stops at rest but rest pain is absent.
questions.explanation: A narrowed vessel may deliver adequate resting flow but cannot dilate enough to meet exercise demand, causing reversible ischaemia.
distractors: Plaque does not disappear with exertion.
Exercise raises myocardial work and oxygen requirements.
Resting coronary flow may be sufficient despite reduced reserve.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.section: 4. Why are the a, c and v waves separated by x and y descents?
questions.stem: What does the normal jugular venous 'v' wave mainly represent?
options: Closure of the pulmonary semilunar valve.
Right atrial electrical depolarisation.
Completion of left ventricular ejection.
Atrial filling while tricuspid is closed.
questions.explanation: Systemic venous return fills the right atrium during ventricular systole while the tricuspid valve remains closed, creating the v wave.
distractors: Pulmonary valve closure is near S2.
Atrial depolarisation precedes the a wave.
The v wave is defined by right atrial filling rather than aortic ejection.

questions.section: 2. The pathway of cardiac electrical conduction
questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces normal electrical conduction from atria into ventricular myocardium?
options: SA node → Purkinje fibres → AV node → His bundle.
SA node → AV node → His bundle → Purkinje fibres.
AV node → SA node → left ventricle → right atrium.
Purkinje fibres → atria → SA node → AV node.
questions.explanation: The SA node initiates impulses that reach the AV node, traverse the His–bundle branches and Purkinje system, then depolarise ventricles.
distractors: Purkinje fibres come after the AV–His pathway.
The SA node normally initiates atrial excitation.
Ventricular Purkinje fibres conduct after, not before, atrial activation.

questions.section: 5. Ejection: why blood finally leaves
questions.stem: What event ends isovolumetric contraction and begins ventricular ejection?
options: Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
Atrial contraction briefly increases end-diastolic volume.
Ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure.
Ventricular pressure exceeds the outflow artery pressure.
questions.explanation: Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic or pulmonary arterial pressure. The pressure reversal is the immediate mechanical trigger for valve opening.
distractors: This pressure relation opens the AV valves during filling.
Atrial systole precedes isovolumetric contraction.
Lower ventricular than aortic pressure holds the aortic valve closed.

questions.section: 2. Why doesn't blood stop moving during diastole?
questions.stem: During ventricular diastole, what would an increase in peripheral resistance do to the rate of aortic pressure decline if compliance were unchanged?
options: Speed the decline by increasing downstream runoff.
Leave the decline unaffected by downstream resistance.
Slow the decline by reducing downstream runoff.
Reverse arterial flow from capillaries toward the aorta.
questions.explanation: Greater downstream resistance reduces diastolic runoff from the elastic arterial reservoir; at unchanged compliance, aortic pressure falls more slowly.
distractors: Greater resistance normally reduces runoff rather than increasing it.
Diastolic decay depends in part on resistance and arterial compliance.
Higher resistance slows forward runoff but does not reverse normal arterial flow.

questions.section: 5. Why do heart sounds change in loudness?
questions.stem: Why may the aortic component of the second heart sound become more prominent in systemic hypertension?
options: Brisk aortic valve closure under higher pressure.
Late mitral valve closure during ventricular relaxation.
Reduced pulmonary resistance delaying right ventricular ejection.
Earlier tricuspid closure following atrial contraction.
questions.explanation: Higher aortic pressure can produce a louder aortic component (A2) of S2 because aortic valve closure is more forceful.
distractors: Mitral closure contributes to S1, not the aortic component of S2.
Pulmonary resistance and right ventricular ejection primarily influence P2 timing.
Tricuspid closure contributes to S1, not A2.

questions.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
questions.section: 7. What changes contractility?
questions.stem: Which condition is most likely to depress myocardial contractility rather than enhance it?
options: Acute beta-1 adrenergic activation.
Raised circulating catecholamines.
Severe hypoxia with acidosis.
Increased calcium availability in cells.
questions.explanation: Severe hypoxia and acidosis impair myocardial function and are listed as causes of depressed inotropy.
distractors: Beta-1 activation generally enhances contractility.
Catecholamines usually raise inotropy initially.
Increased cytosolic calcium generally enhances contraction.

questions.section: 7. What changes microvascular filtration or permeability?
questions.stem: A local inflammatory mediator increases postcapillary venular permeability. What occurs?
options: More protein and water can escape, promoting tissue swelling.
The vascular wall becomes impermeable to water.
The plasma protein concentration increases within the vessel.
Capillary filtration stops until arterial pressure rises.
questions.explanation: Higher permeability permits protein extravasation and fluid movement, weakening oncotic retention and promoting oedema.
distractors: Inflammation generally increases rather than abolishes permeability.
Protein leakage tends to lower intravascular protein in the affected region.
Fluid escape is promoted, not stopped.

questions.section: 6. What does central venous pressure tell us?
questions.stem: A patient's right ventricular pumping fails and right atrial pressure rises. Which consequence is most likely?
options: A larger pressure gradient for systemic venous return.
Reduced congestion in peripheral systemic veins.
Reduced venous return gradient with congestion.
Complete disappearance of the jugular venous pulse.
questions.explanation: Higher right atrial pressure opposes venous return and transmits backward into systemic veins, causing congestion.
distractors: Higher right atrial pressure reduces the upstream-to-atrial gradient.
Elevated atrial pressure tends to increase congestion.
JVP often becomes elevated rather than disappearing.

questions.stem: Where is the largest controllable fall in systemic vascular pressure normally produced?
options: Across the venae cavae.
Within the right atrium alone.
Across resistance arterioles.
Across large elastic arteries.
questions.explanation: Small arteries and arterioles provide substantial resistance, producing a major pressure drop from arterial to capillary levels.
distractors: Large veins carry blood at low pressure and resistance.
Right atrial pressure is low but does not create the main distributed arterial drop.
Large elastic arteries conduct flow with relatively small resistance.

questions.stem: During a stress response, circulating adrenaline dilates vessels in working skeletal muscle while constricting many skin vessels. Why?
options: The muscle vessels lack any adrenergic receptors.
Different vascular beds express different adrenergic receptors.
Skin tissue receives a much lower concentration of adrenaline.
Different vascular beds contain markedly different amounts of plasma.
questions.explanation: β₂ effects can favour dilation in skeletal muscle, while α₁ effects cause constriction in many skin and gut vessels.
distractors: Muscle vessels respond because they possess adrenergic receptors.
The difference is due mainly to receptor distribution rather than selective circulating delivery.
Plasma volume differences do not explain opposite receptor responses.

questions.stem: A recording shows that cardiac vagal stimulation lowers the firing rate of the sinoatrial node. Which additional effect is expected?
options: Stronger ventricular contraction through beta-1 activation.
Faster impulse conduction through the AV node.
Slower impulse conduction through the AV node.
Faster pacemaker discharge through alpha-1 activation.
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic acetylcholine acts at muscarinic M₂ receptors to slow both SA nodal firing and AV nodal conduction.
distractors: β₁ activation describes sympathetic, not vagal, stimulation.
AV conduction is slowed rather than accelerated by vagal action.
The major cardiac pacemaker effect is not mediated by α₁.

questions.stem: Electrical stimulation of the medullary pressor area increases arterial pressure. What is the principal neural pathway?
options: Direct stimulation of the carotid sinus sensory fibres.
Inhibition of sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord.
Direct inhibition of firing in the sinoatrial pacemaker.
Excitation of sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The pressor area sends excitatory fibres down to the sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord. More sympathetic output constricts arterioles and veins and speeds and strengthens the heart, so pressure rises.
distractors: Carotid sinus fibres carry sensory information towards the medulla.
Inhibiting sympathetic neurons would tend to lower pressure.
Pressor-area activity does not require direct pacemaker inhibition.

questions.section: 4. How the body fights back
questions.stem: Immediately after rapid loss of a large volume of whole blood, haemoglobin concentration is unexpectedly unchanged. Why?
options: Red-cell mass increases enough to compensate.
Plasma enters faster than red cells are lost.
Red cells and plasma were lost together.
Erythropoietin instantly makes new red cells.
questions.explanation: Acute whole-blood loss removes red cells and plasma proportionately, so concentration may remain unchanged before fluid replacement.
distractors: Red-cell mass falls with whole-blood loss.
Early dilution has not yet occurred in this scenario.
Erythropoiesis takes days to weeks, not minutes.

questions.stem: A patient with left-sided heart failure feels breathless when lying flat but improves after sitting up. Why?
options: Lying flat shifts peripheral blood toward congested lungs.
Lying flat reduces central blood volume.
Sitting up directly increases pulmonary capillary pressure.
Sitting up increases venous return from the legs.
questions.explanation: Supine positioning returns peripheral blood to the thorax; a failing left ventricle cannot handle the extra flow, increasing pulmonary venous congestion.
distractors: Central thoracic volume commonly increases rather than decreases supine.
A higher pulmonary capillary pressure would worsen breathlessness.
Sitting upright tends to reduce thoracic venous return.

questions.stem: What can follow when the right ventricle fails to deliver adequate forward flow to the lungs?
options: Pulmonary flow rises despite low right ventricular output.
Less blood reaches the left heart for systemic output.
Systemic tissues receive more oxygen-rich blood immediately.
Left ventricular filling necessarily increases sharply.
questions.explanation: Reduced right ventricular output limits pulmonary flow and subsequent return to the left atrium, compromising left-sided filling and delivery.
distractors: The right heart cannot deliver excess flow when severely failing.
Reduced pulmonary transit cannot raise systemic oxygen delivery.
Less pulmonary venous return tends to decrease left-sided filling.

questions.stem: In severe haemorrhagic shock, why does sympathetic constriction of splanchnic vessels help initially?
options: It increases flow to the intestinal mucosa above baseline.
It increases hepatic oxygen extraction to 100%.
It prevents all intestinal ischaemia during shock.
It redistributes flow and mobilises stored venous blood.
questions.explanation: The splanchnic bed is a large blood reservoir; vasoconstriction redirects perfusion and recruits stored blood toward central circulation.
distractors: Mucosal flow may decrease, risking ischaemia.
Extraction is not necessarily complete.
Severe or prolonged constriction can contribute to intestinal injury.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 5. The coverings, the ventricles and CSF
questions.stem: A patient has hydrocephalus due to impaired absorption by arachnoid villi without an obstructed ventricular pathway. What type is this?
options: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus.
Obstructive aqueductal hydrocephalus.
Communicating hydrocephalus.
Isolated ventricular haemorrhage.
questions.explanation: Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when CSF reaches subarachnoid space but reabsorption is impaired. The ventricular pathway remains open, so the defect is in absorption rather than transit.
distractors: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus results from blocked ventricular drainage.
Aqueductal stenosis is a specific obstruction.
Haemorrhage may contribute to hydrocephalus but is not the classification described.

questions.chapter: Chapter 27 — Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth
questions.section: 2. Trace the fetal circuit
questions.stem: Where does the ductus arteriosus carry much fetal right ventricular output?
options: Directly from right atrium to left atrium.
From pulmonary trunk into descending aorta.
From left ventricle into hepatic portal vein.
From umbilical vein into inferior vena cava.
questions.explanation: High prenatal pulmonary resistance diverts much right ventricular output through ductus arteriosus into the aorta.
distractors: Right-to-left atrial passage occurs at the foramen ovale.
Left ventricular output does not enter the portal vein.
Umbilical venous diversion occurs at the ductus venosus.

questions.section: 1. Two circulations in one lung
questions.stem: Why can some oxygenated bronchial venous drainage slightly lower oxygen content of blood reaching the left atrium?
options: Bronchial venous blood drains only into the superior vena cava.
Some bronchial venous blood joins pulmonary veins.
Bronchial arteries arise directly from right ventricle.
Pulmonary arterial blood bypasses alveolar capillaries entirely.
questions.explanation: Some bronchial venous return enters pulmonary veins, mixing a small amount of deoxygenated blood with oxygenated pulmonary venous blood.
distractors: Not all bronchial venous blood returns only through systemic veins.
Bronchial arteries arise from the systemic arterial circulation.
Normal pulmonary blood passes through alveolar capillary networks.

questions.section: 7. Calculate heart rate from the tracing
questions.stem: An irregular tracing contains eleven QRS complexes in a six-second span. What is the estimated average ventricular rate?
options: 66 beats/min.
90 beats/min.
100 beats/min.
110 beats/min.
questions.explanation: Six seconds is one tenth of a minute. Eleven QRS complexes over that span give an approximate average ventricular rate of 11 × 10 = 110 beats/min.
distractors: This multiplies the QRS count by six, not by ten.
A rate of 90 beats/min would correspond to nine complexes in six seconds.
A rate of 100 beats/min would correspond to ten complexes in six seconds.

notes: Three distinct 60-question papers. Each contains 40 reviewed core questions and 20 redistributed/replacement questions. Weak items swapped using unselected 328-item lecture bank. Original five-option items standardized by removing a distractor. Further precision checks and balanced answer repositioning are planned.
